Here is the version that does have an answer. Replace the light fronts with two spaceships leaving you at $0.9c$ in opposite directions. In your frame the gap between them grows at $1.8c$: still fine, because it is a gap, not a ship. But the relative velocity of one ship measured by the other comes from the relativistic velocity addition equation, $u' = \dfrac{u - v}{1 - \dfrac{uv}{c^2}}$, with $u = 0.9c$ for the right-hand ship and $v = -0.9c$ for the frame of the left-hand ship: $u' = \dfrac{0.9c + 0.9c}{1 + 0.81} = \dfrac{1.8c}{1.81} = 0.994c$. Each ship measures the other moving away at $0.994c$, below $c$ as it must be. The nearer the ships get to $c$, the nearer this result gets to $c$; it never reaches it.
tempting:
"300 000 km, because nothing can separate faster than $c$" misapplies the speed limit to a separation. In one frame you simply add up what each light front did: 300 000 km each way. Nothing in relativity stops two objects being 600 000 km apart after one second.

"Each measures the other at $2c$" is Galilean velocity addition, $u' = u - v$, which fails near $c$. For two spaceships the relativistic equation gives $0.994c$, not $1.8c$.

"Each measures the other at $c$" sounds like the second postulate at work, and would be right if the question were about a spaceship measuring the speed of the light. But it asks what the light itself measures, and light has no frame in which to measure anything. Spotting a question that has no answer is part of understanding the postulates.

title: The plank and the drill

figure.alt: Two panels. Top, labelled 'Drill's frame': a drill at rest with its 10 cm bit pointing right, and a thin plank, 8.7 cm thick, flying towards it at 0.9c. Bottom, labelled 'Plank's frame': a plank 20 cm thick at rest, and a squashed drill with a 4.4 cm bit flying towards it at 0.9c.
figure.caption: The same event seen from the two frames. In the drill's frame (top) the plank is thinner than the bit is long; in the plank's frame (bottom) the bit is much shorter than the plank is thick. Drawn to the same scale.

question: A drill bit is 10 cm long. A plank is 20 cm thick. The drill is held still with its bit pointing along a track, and the plank is fired along the track at $0.9c$, face first, so that the plank's own motion drives the bit into it (assume the bit cuts freely and does not break). In the drill's frame the moving plank is length-contracted to $\dfrac{20}{\gamma} = 8.7$ cm, thinner than the bit, so the tip of the bit pokes out of the plank's far face before the plank reaches the drill's body, and at that instant the drill is flicked sideways out of the plank's path. In the plank's frame, however, the plank is 20 cm thick and it is the drill that is contracted, to 4.4 cm, far shorter than the plank is thick. Is there a hole right through the plank?
options: Yes: the hole goes right through in both frames
The hole goes right through in the drill's frame, but in the plank's frame it is only 4.4 cm deep
A hole cannot go right through in one frame and only part-way in another, so the set-up is impossible: relativity forbids it
In the plank's frame the short bit would snap, so the hole goes through only in the drill's frame
reveal:
The hole goes right through in both frames. Whether the plank has a hole in it is a fact about events (the tip of the bit passing each face of the plank), and events happen in every frame. Observers disagree about when and in what order things happen, never about whether they happen.

In the drill's frame the story is easy: a plank only 8.7 cm thick slides over a 10 cm bit, the tip emerges from the far face, and the drill is flicked aside with 1.3 cm to spare. Hole.

In the plank's frame the plank sits still, 20 cm thick, and a 4.4 cm bit arrives at $0.9c$. A short bit can still make a long hole, just as a short bullet goes right through a thick wall: the tip enters the front face and keeps moving at $0.9c$ until it comes out of the back face, 20 cm later. The puzzle is the drill's body, which is now only 4.4 cm behind the tip. Doesn't it hit the plank long before the tip gets through? Here the relativity of simultaneity does the work. "Flick the whole drill sideways" happens at one instant in the drill's frame, but the drill's body and the bit's tip are in different places, so in the plank's frame those two flicks are not simultaneous: the body is flicked aside first, while it is still about 3 cm short of the plank, and the tip is flicked only after it has travelled another 18.6 cm and emerged from the back face. For that moment, in the plank's frame, the drill is bent: its body has moved aside while its tip is still boring through the wood. Nothing is rigid in relativity, because no part of an object can find out what another part is doing faster than light.

Two numbers to check: $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 0.9^2}} = 2.29$, so $L = \dfrac{L_0}{\gamma}$ gives $20/2.29 = 8.7$ cm for the plank in the drill's frame and $10/2.29 = 4.4$ cm for the drill in the plank's frame. The two "flick" events are 10 cm apart in the drill's frame and happen together there, so the Lorentz transformation $t' = \gamma\left(t - \dfrac{vx}{c^2}\right)$ puts them $\gamma \times 0.9 \times 10 = 20.6$ cm of light-travel time apart in the plank's frame, during which the tip, at $0.9c$, covers $0.9 \times 20.6 = 18.6$ cm. This is the pole-and-barn paradox (a long pole that fits inside a short barn in one frame but not the other) with a twist, and it is resolved the same way: both frames agree on every event, and only their ordering in time differs.
tempting:
"Only 4.4 cm deep in the plank's frame" treats the contracted drill as if it were stationary: a 4.4 cm bit pushed gently into a plank would stop at 4.4 cm. But in the plank's frame the bit is moving at $0.9c$; its tip goes wherever its motion carries it, right out of the far side.

"Relativity forbids it" is the right instinct applied to the wrong thing. Relativity does forbid a hole that exists in one frame and not in another, because the hole is made of events. It therefore requires the plank's frame to find a way for the hole to go through, and the relativity of simultaneity provides it. A set-up that seems to give two frames different facts is a sign that you have assumed something is simultaneous, or rigid, when it is not.

"The short bit would snap" imagines length contraction as a physical squashing that strains the material. It is not: the drill is at rest in its own frame and perfectly comfortable. Its length in another frame is a different measurement, not a different drill.

title: Twice as hot

figure.alt: Two glasses of the same water, each with a thermometer. The left glass, labelled now, reads 10 degrees Celsius. The right glass, labelled twice as hot, has its reading replaced by a question mark.

question: Some water in a glass is at 10 °C. Suppose "twice as hot" means that its molecules have twice the average random kinetic energy. What temperature would the water have to reach? (Ignore boiling: assume the water is kept under enough pressure to stay liquid.)
reveal:
The average random kinetic energy of the molecules is proportional to the kelvin temperature, not the Celsius temperature. So convert first: $T = 10 + 273 = 283$ K.

Twice the average kinetic energy needs twice the kelvin temperature: $2 \times 283 = 566$ K. Converting back, $566 - 273 = 293$ °C. "Twice as hot" in this sense is 293 °C.

Heating the water to 20 °C (293 K) only multiplies the average kinetic energy by $\dfrac{293}{283} = 1.04$: an increase of about 4%.
tempting:
"Twice as hot" sounds like "twice the number", so 20 °C is tempting. But the zero of the Celsius scale is just the temperature at which water freezes, and the molecules at 0 °C are still moving fast. The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, where (in the kinetic model) the particles have no random kinetic energy at all. That's why only kelvin temperatures can be doubled or halved like this.

566 °C comes from doubling correctly in kelvin but forgetting to convert back to Celsius. 273 °C (546 K) doubles the 273 K of melting ice and leaves out the 10 °C.

title: Copper or wood on ice

figure.alt: A small copper cube and a larger wooden block, each resting on its own block of ice. Both have a mass of 0.20 kg and a temperature of 100 degrees Celsius.
figure.caption: Drawn roughly to scale: the masses are equal, but wood is much less dense than copper.

question: A 0.20 kg block of copper and a 0.20 kg block of dry wood are both heated to 100 °C. Each is then placed on its own large block of ice at 0 °C and left until it has cooled to 0 °C. No energy is transferred to or from the air, and neither block of ice melts completely. Which block melts more ice? (Specific heat capacities: copper 390 $\text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$, dry wood about 1700 $\text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$.)
options: The copper
The wood
They melt the same amount
It depends on how fast each one conducts
reveal:
The wood melts more than four times as much ice as the copper. As each block cools by 100 K it gives out energy $Q = mc\Delta T$, and all of that energy melts ice at 0 °C. The mass of ice melted is $\dfrac{Q}{L_f}$, with $L_f = 3.34 \times 10^5$ $\text{J kg}^{-1}$.

  • Copper ($c = 390$ $\text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$): $Q = 0.20 \times 390 \times 100 = 7800$ J, which melts $\dfrac{7800}{3.34 \times 10^5} = 0.023$ kg, about 23 g of ice.
  • Dry wood ($c \approx 1700$ $\text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$): $Q = 0.20 \times 1700 \times 100 = 34\,000$ J, which melts $\dfrac{34\,000}{3.34 \times 10^5} = 0.10$ kg, about 100 g of ice.

The masses and the temperature drops are the same, so the difference comes entirely from the specific heat capacity. Wood's is more than four times copper's, so it gives out more than four times as much energy for every kelvin it cools.
tempting:
Copper at 100 °C feels much hotter to touch than wood at 100 °C, and it melts its way into the ice much more quickly, so it seems to hold more "heat". But conduction decides how fast energy is transferred, not how much is transferred in total. The copper melts its 23 g quickly; the wood melts its 100 g slowly, but it gets there in the end. That's why "it depends on how fast each one conducts" is wrong: it mixes up the rate of transfer with the total energy.

It's also tempting to think that equal masses at equal temperatures must give out equal amounts of energy. Temperature tells you which way energy will flow; how much flows also depends on $m$ and $c$.

title: Sparks and the baking tray

figure.alt: Left: a lit sparkler throwing out sparks, labelled over 1000 degrees Celsius. Right: a baking tray of biscuits straight from the oven, labelled 200 degrees Celsius.

question: The sparks from a sparkler can be hotter than 1000 °C, yet a spark that lands on your hand barely hurts. A baking tray at 200 °C, straight from the oven, burns you if you touch it. Why? (Don't test either one: a sparkler's wire stays dangerously hot.)
reveal:
Temperature alone doesn't decide how much energy reaches your skin. The mass and specific heat capacity of the hot object matter, and so does how quickly energy can keep arriving.

A spark is a tiny particle of burning iron (much of it iron oxide by the time it lands), with a mass of perhaps 0.1 mg, which is $1 \times 10^{-7}$ kg. With $c \approx 650$ $\text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$, cooling it by about 1000 K releases only

$$Q = mc\Delta T = 1 \times 10^{-7} \times 650 \times 1000 \approx 0.065\ \text{J}$$

Shared with just 5 mg of skin (mostly water, $c \approx 4200$ $\text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$), that would warm it by about $\dfrac{0.065}{5 \times 10^{-6} \times 4200} \approx 3$ K. In fact the spark has already lost much of its energy to the air on the way down. Its temperature falls almost at once, and there is no more energy behind it.

A baking tray of, say, 0.5 kg of steel ($c \approx 450$ $\text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$) gives out about $0.5 \times 450 \times 160 = 36\,000$ J as it cools to 40 °C: around half a million times as much. Metal is also a good conductor, so as your skin takes energy from the spot you touch, energy flows in from the rest of the tray and keeps that spot close to 200 °C. Your skin is heated to a damaging temperature very quickly.
tempting:
It's tempting to think that the hotter object must always do more harm, as if temperature were "the amount of heat". But temperature measures the average random kinetic energy of the particles, not the total. A spark has so few particles that its internal energy is tiny, however high its temperature.

The same idea explains why the air inside a 200 °C oven doesn't burn your hand at once, though the tray does: the air has a very small mass and is a poor conductor.

title: Milk now or later?

figure.alt: A steaming cup of hot coffee and a small jug of cold milk on a table, with a clock marking a five-minute wait.
figure.caption: You must wait five minutes before drinking.

question: You have just made a cup of hot coffee, and a small jug of cold milk is on the table beside it. You must leave the cup for five minutes before you drink it. You will add the milk at some point, and you want the drink to be as hot as possible when you finally drink it. The room is cooler than both the coffee and the milk, and the milk stays at its own temperature while it waits in the jug. Should you add the milk now, or just before you drink?
options: Add the milk now
Add the milk just before drinking
It makes no difference
reveal:
Add the milk now, although the gain is small.

The coffee loses energy to the room by conduction and convection into the air (and the cup), by thermal radiation, and by evaporation from the surface. For every one of these, the rate of energy transfer is larger when the drink is hotter: the rate of conduction is proportional to the temperature difference between the drink and its surroundings, a hotter surface drives faster convection, and a hotter surface radiates more. So the hotter the drink is during the wait, the faster it loses energy.

Adding the milk now makes the drink cooler at the start of the five minutes, so it loses energy more slowly for the whole wait. Leaving the coffee black keeps it hotter, so it loses more energy, and then the same cold milk cools it by the same amount at the end. The "milk now" cup wins both ways: it loses less energy during the wait, and it has more mass, so a given energy loss lowers its temperature by less ($Q = mc\Delta T$).

Numbers show how small the effect is. Suppose 200 g of coffee at 90 °C and 50 g of milk at 5 °C (treat both as water), in a room at 20 °C, and suppose that black coffee would cool from 90 °C to 75 °C in the five minutes. Milk now: the mixture starts at $\dfrac{4 \times 90 + 1 \times 5}{5} = 73$ °C, and cooling at a rate proportional to the temperature difference above the room (Newton's law of cooling, beyond the course) brings it to about 61.6 °C if the milky cup cooled at the same rate per degree as the black one; allowing for its extra 50 g, which makes its temperature fall more slowly for the same energy loss, gives about 63.7 °C. Milk later: the coffee is at 75 °C, and adding the milk gives $\dfrac{4 \times 75 + 1 \times 5}{5} = 61$ °C. So between half a degree and about three degrees in favour of "now". In a real kitchen the milk in the jug warms slightly towards room temperature while it waits, which helps "later" and makes the difference smaller still. Physics says "now"; your tongue may not notice.
tempting:
"It makes no difference" is the natural answer: the same milk goes into the same coffee either way, so surely the final temperature is the same. That would be true if the coffee lost energy at a fixed rate, whatever its temperature. But the rate of cooling depends on the temperature difference between the drink and the room, so a hotter drink loses more energy in the same five minutes. The order matters.

"Just before drinking" comes from the feeling that cold milk "ruins" a hot drink, so it should go in as late as possible. The milk lowers the temperature by the same amount whenever it goes in; what differs is how much energy the drink loses to the room in the meantime, and that is smaller for the cooler, milky drink.

title: The pot inside the pot

figure.alt: A small metal pot of water sits inside a large pot of water on a gas flame. The water in the large pot has bubbles and is boiling; the water in the small pot has none.
figure.caption: The outer water boils hard; the inner water never does. Not to scale.

question: A large metal pot of water is boiling vigorously on a hob at normal atmospheric pressure. A small, thin metal pot, also holding water, sits inside it so that its base and sides are surrounded by the boiling water. The inner water gets very hot, but however long you wait and however hard the outer water boils, the inner water never boils. Why not?
options: The inner water stays well below 100 °C
The inner water reaches 100 °C but then receives no more energy
The metal of the small pot stops thermal energy getting through
Water in a pot inside a pot needs to be hotter than 100 °C to boil
reveal:
The inner water reaches 100 °C, but then it receives no more energy.

Energy is transferred by conduction through the thin metal wall only while there is a temperature difference across it: the rate of transfer is proportional to the temperature difference. At first the outer water (100 °C) is hotter than the inner water, so energy flows in and the inner water warms up. When the inner water reaches 100 °C it is in thermal equilibrium with the boiling water around it: both are at the same temperature, so there is no net transfer of energy and the inner water goes no further.

To boil, that is not enough. Boiling is a change of state at a constant temperature, and it needs a continuous supply of energy: the specific latent heat of vaporization of water is $L_v = 2.26 \times 10^6$ $\text{J kg}^{-1}$, so turning just 0.50 kg of the inner water into steam would need $Q = mL = 0.50 \times 2.26 \times 10^6 = 1.1 \times 10^6$ J. The outer water can boil because the flame keeps pushing energy into it; the inner water has no source hotter than itself, so it can only sit at 100 °C.

Meanwhile the outer water stays at 100 °C no matter how fiercely it boils: a hotter flame makes it boil faster, not hotter. That is why no amount of extra heat under the big pot helps. (Cooks use exactly this arrangement, a bain-marie, to warm delicate sauces without ever boiling them.)
tempting:
"It never reaches 100 °C" sounds cautious, but there is no reason for it to stop short: energy keeps flowing in while the inner water is cooler than the outer water, and the outer water stays at 100 °C. The inner water does get to 100 °C; the problem comes after that.

"The metal stops the energy getting through" has it backwards. Metals are good thermal conductors, and the inner water clearly gets very hot, so energy is getting through. The wall is not the barrier; the lack of a temperature difference is.

"It needs to be hotter than 100 °C" confuses two things. At normal pressure water boils at 100 °C wherever it is. What it needs is not a higher temperature but a continuing supply of energy at that temperature, to pay the latent heat of vaporization.

title: Who is glowing?

figure.alt: A dark room drawn in outline: a fire poker leaning against the wall on the left, a person standing in the middle, and a block of ice on the right. Nothing in the picture shows any radiation.
figure.caption: A poker, a person and a block of ice, in a room with the lights off.

question: Three things are in a dark room: a poker just taken from a fire, with its tip red hot at about 1000 K; a person at about 310 K; and a block of ice at 273 K. Which of the three emit electromagnetic radiation? Decide, and say what kind of radiation each one gives off, if any.
reveal:
All three emit electromagnetic radiation, all the time. Every object with a temperature above absolute zero radiates; the temperature decides how much and at which wavelengths.

Wien's displacement law, $\lambda_{\text{max}} T = 2.9 \times 10^{-3}$ m K, gives the wavelength at which each one radiates most strongly. The poker at 1000 K peaks at $\lambda_{\text{max}} = \dfrac{2.9 \times 10^{-3}}{1000} = 2.9$ μm, in the infrared, but its spectrum has a tail into the red end of the visible range: that is the red glow you see. The person at 310 K peaks at $\dfrac{2.9 \times 10^{-3}}{310} = 9.4$ μm, far infrared, which eyes cannot see but a thermal camera shows clearly. The ice at 273 K peaks at $\dfrac{2.9 \times 10^{-3}}{273} = 10.6$ μm, a little further into the infrared still.

The Stefan–Boltzmann law, $L = \sigma A T^4$ (for a black body, which all three roughly are), gives the power. Per square metre, taking emissivity $e \approx 1$ for all three, the poker radiates $5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times 1000^4 \approx 57\,000$ $\text{W m}^{-2}$, the person about $5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times 310^4 \approx 520$ $\text{W m}^{-2}$, and the ice about $5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times 273^4 \approx 315$ $\text{W m}^{-2}$. The ice radiates $\left(\dfrac{273}{310}\right)^4 = 0.60$ times as much per square metre as the person: cold, but far from dark. (Net energy flow is another matter: the ice also absorbs radiation from the warmer room, and absorbs more than it emits, so it slowly warms and melts.)

Nothing glows visibly until it is hot enough for the short-wavelength tail of its spectrum to reach the visible range, at roughly 800 K (beyond the course, but a useful landmark): that is the dull red of the poker. Hotter still and the glow turns orange, yellow and white.
tempting:
"Only the poker: only hot things glow" confuses visible glow with radiation. Visible glow needs a temperature above about 800 K, but emission never stops; it just moves to longer wavelengths as the object cools. A thermal camera makes the invisible glow of a person, or of a wall, obvious.

"Ice is cold, so it absorbs rather than emits" treats absorbing and emitting as opposites. Every surface does both at once. The ice emits according to its own temperature and absorbs according to what falls on it. In a warm room the absorbed power is larger, so the net flow is into the ice, but the ice is still radiating at about 315 $\text{W m}^{-2}$ the whole time.

title: A candle in free fall

figure.alt: Left: a candle on a table with its usual tall teardrop flame, labelled on Earth. Right: an identical candle seen through the porthole of an orbiting module, labelled in orbit, with a question mark where its flame would be.
figure.caption: The same candle on Earth and in an orbiting module. What does the flame on the right look like?

question: A candle is lit inside a sealed, air-filled module orbiting the Earth. Everything in the module is in continuous free fall, so the air and the hot gases are effectively weightless. Predict how the flame differs from a candle flame on Earth: its shape, its colour and brightness, and whether it keeps burning.
reveal:
The flame becomes a small, dim, blue sphere around the wick, burns slowly, and may go out. NASA has burned candles on the Space Shuttle and on the Russian space station Mir to see exactly this.

On Earth a flame's shape comes from convection. The hot gases around the wick are less dense than the surrounding air, so the buoyancy force on them, $F_{\text{b}} = \rho V g$, is larger than their weight and they rise. That upward stream draws them into a tall teardrop and pulls fresh, oxygen-rich air in at the bottom. The yellow light is thermal radiation from tiny hot soot particles carried up through the flame.

In free fall there is no "up" for buoyancy to work with: the buoyancy force and the weight both depend on $g$, and in the module's frame the effective $g$ is zero, so both disappear: there is no pressure difference in the air to push the hot gases anywhere, and they do not rise. No convection means no draught: the burnt gases stay around the wick and fresh oxygen can only reach the flame by molecules spreading through the gas on their own (diffusion, beyond the course in name, but just random molecular motion). The flame spreads out evenly in all directions as a sphere, burns much more slowly, and is cooler, so little soot forms and there is no yellow glow: only the faint blue light of the burning gas. In a closed space the slow supply of oxygen often lets the flame starve and go out, which is one reason fire on a spacecraft behaves so differently and is studied so carefully.

revealFigure.alt: Left: the Earth candle with its tall yellow flame. Right: the orbiting candle with a small, faint blue sphere of flame around the wick.
revealFigure.caption: On Earth, convection stretches the flame upwards. In orbit, with no convection, the flame is a small blue sphere. Not to scale.

tempting:
"There is no gravity, so there is no flame" is wrong twice over. Gravity in low orbit is only about 10% weaker than at the surface; the module and everything in it are in free fall, which is why things float. And a flame needs fuel, oxygen and heat, not gravity: the candle lights perfectly well.

"The flame is the same" ignores how much of a flame's familiar look depends on hot gas rising. Take away convection and the shape, colour, brightness and burning rate all change.

"It goes out at once" is too quick. The flame burns steadily, if slowly, for as long as diffusion brings enough oxygen to the wick; candles on Mir burned for many minutes, some for about three-quarters of an hour, before fading.

title: Ice meets boiling water

figure.alt: A tilted jug of steaming water pours into an open box with thick insulated walls. Inside the box are several ice cubes. Labels: 1 kg water at 100 °C, 1 kg ice at 0 °C, insulated box.
figure.caption: The hot water is poured onto the ice and the box is closed. Not to scale.

question: 1.0 kg of ice at 0 °C is put in a well-insulated box, and 1.0 kg of water at 100 °C is poured over it. The box is closed and left until everything inside is at one temperature. No energy is transferred to or from the box or the surroundings. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 $\text{J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$ and the specific latent heat of fusion of ice is $3.34 \times 10^5$ $\text{J kg}^{-1}$. What is the final temperature?
options: 0 °C, with some ice left
About 10 °C
About 25 °C
reveal:
About 10 °C. Melting the ice swallows most of the hot water's energy before any warming can start.

First check that all the ice melts. Melting 1.0 kg of ice needs $Q = mL = 1.0 \times 3.34 \times 10^5 = 3.34 \times 10^5$ J. The hot water can give up $Q = mc\Delta T = 1.0 \times 4200 \times 100 = 4.2 \times 10^5$ J before it reaches 0 °C, which is more than enough, so the ice does all melt and the final temperature is above 0 °C.

Now find it. Melting the ice cools the hot water by $\Delta T = \dfrac{3.34 \times 10^5}{4200} = 79.5$ K, to 20.5 °C. That leaves 1.0 kg of water at 0 °C (the melted ice) and 1.0 kg at 20.5 °C, which mix to $\dfrac{0 + 20.5}{2} = 10.2$ °C. In one line: energy lost by the hot water = energy gained by the ice, $4200(100 - T) = 3.34 \times 10^5 + 4200\,T$, so $8400\,T = 8.6 \times 10^4$ and $T = 10.2$ °C.

The reason the answer is so low is that a phase change happens at constant temperature: the energy that melts the ice goes into pulling the molecules apart from their fixed positions, raising their intermolecular potential energy, not into making them move faster. Only after that does any energy go into raising the temperature, which is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the molecules. The same 1.0 kg of cold water at 0 °C, instead of ice, would have given 50 °C.
tempting:
"50 °C" is the average of 0 and 100, and it would be right for equal masses of water at those temperatures. It forgets the latent heat: ice at 0 °C must first be melted, and that costs as much energy as cooling the hot water by almost 80 K, before the melted ice has warmed by a single degree.

"0 °C with some ice left" takes the latent heat seriously but over-estimates it. The numbers settle it: the hot water has $4.2 \times 10^5$ J to give before it reaches 0 °C, and melting all the ice needs only $3.34 \times 10^5$ J. Ice would be left over only if the hot water had less than about 0.8 kg, or started cooler than about 80 °C.

"About 25 °C" is a compromise between the two: latent heat matters, so knock the 50 °C down a bit. Guessing the size of the effect is risky; a quick $Q = mL$ and $Q = mc\Delta T$ shows that melting costs the equivalent of almost 80 K of cooling, not 25 K.

title: The heated ring

figure.alt: A flat metal washer lies on a tripod above a Bunsen burner flame. To the left, the same washer is drawn seen from above, a ring with a round hole in the middle.
figure.caption: A flat metal washer is heated evenly on a tripod. On the left, the same washer seen from above. Not to scale.

question: A flat metal washer, a disc with a round hole in the middle, is heated evenly on a tripod until the whole washer is at the same high temperature. Metals expand slightly when they are heated. What happens to the diameter of the hole?
options: It gets bigger
It gets smaller
It stays the same size
reveal:
The hole gets bigger. Every part of the washer grows, including the empty part.

Heating a solid gives its atoms more kinetic energy (temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles), so they vibrate more vigorously about their positions, and the average distance between neighbouring atoms grows by a small fraction. The key point is that every distance between two atoms in the washer grows by the same fraction, wherever they are. So the whole washer scales up like a photograph being enlarged, and the gap between the atoms on opposite sides of the hole grows by the same fraction as everything else.

Another way to see it: a washer is a rod bent into a circle. When the rod is heated its length grows, so the circumference of the ring grows, and since $C = 2\pi r$, so does the radius of the hole. (The ring cannot grow a longer circumference while its hole shrinks.) Or imagine drawing a circle on a flat metal sheet and then heating the sheet: the drawn circle grows. Cutting out the metal inside the circle changes nothing about how the rest expands.

The effect is small: steel grows by about one part in a hundred thousand for every kelvin, so a 20 mm hole heated by 300 K grows by about 0.07 mm. That is enough to matter: it is why a metal lid stuck on a glass jar loosens under hot water (the lid expands more than the glass), how engineers fit a wheel onto an axle by heating the wheel first, and why bridges and railway tracks have expansion gaps. (Thermal expansion itself is beyond the IB course; the link to B.1 is temperature as a measure of molecular kinetic energy and the larger average spacing of atoms that vibrate harder.)

revealFigure.alt: Two rings drawn on the same centre. A dashed blue ring shows the cold washer. A solid orange ring, slightly larger in both its outer edge and its hole, shows the hot washer.
revealFigure.caption: The cold washer and the hot washer, hugely exaggerated: the real change is a fraction of a millimetre. The outer edge and the hole both grow by the same fraction.

tempting:
"It gets smaller" treats the hole as empty space waiting to be filled, as if the metal expands inwards into it, growing in every direction from its own middle. But expansion is not the metal "pushing out" into whatever space is nearest; it is every atom moving slightly further from its neighbours. Neighbouring atoms around the inner edge move further apart from each other, so the inner edge gets longer, and a longer circle is a bigger circle.

"It stays the same size" imagines an inward expansion and an outward expansion fighting over the hole. There is only one expansion, by one scale factor, applied to every length in the washer: the outer diameter, the width of the metal and the hole all grow by the same fraction. If you have ever struggled with a jar lid, you have already seen that the hole in a heated ring gets bigger.

title: Clear and cloudy nights

figure.alt: Two night scenes with the same house and a thermometer marked with a question mark. Left: a clear sky with stars and the Moon. Right: low clouds covering the sky.

question: Two winter nights start at the same temperature at sunset, with no wind. One night is cloudless; the other has a thick layer of low cloud. By morning, the ground has cooled much more on the cloudless night, often enough for frost to form. Why do the clouds make such a difference?
reveal:
Clouds absorb the infrared radiation emitted by the ground, and send much of it back down.

At night there is no sunlight, but the ground keeps emitting infrared radiation, as every object above absolute zero does. Whether it cools depends on the balance between the infrared it emits and the infrared it receives from the sky.

  • Clear night: a good part of the ground's infrared passes straight through the dry air and escapes to space. The sky sends back relatively little, so the ground loses energy quickly and cools.
  • Cloudy night: the water droplets in a cloud absorb almost all the infrared that reaches them. Low cloud is only a little colder than the ground, so its underside emits nearly as much infrared back down as the ground sends up. The ground's net loss is small.

Rough numbers: ground at 5 °C (emissivity 0.95) emits about 320 $\text{W m}^{-2}$. A clear winter sky might send back about 210 $\text{W m}^{-2}$, of which the ground absorbs about 200, so it loses a net 120 $\text{W m}^{-2}$. Low cloud at 0 °C sends back about 310 $\text{W m}^{-2}$, of which the ground absorbs about 295, so the net loss is only about 25 $\text{W m}^{-2}$: around a fifth as much.

This is the same physics as the greenhouse effect: water vapour and cloud droplets absorb infrared and re-emit it in all directions, including back to the surface.

revealFigure.alt: Left, clear night: infrared arrows go up from the ground and out to space. Right, cloudy night: infrared arrows go up from the ground into the cloud; dashed arrows come back down from the cloud to the ground, and one dashed arrow goes up from the top of the cloud.
revealFigure.caption: Infrared emitted by the ground. On a clear night much of it escapes to space. On a cloudy night the cloud absorbs it and emits infrared of its own (dashed), much of it back down to the ground.

tempting:
"Clouds act like a blanket" is a handy picture, but it hides the mechanism and suggests that clouds trap warm air. Clouds are hundreds of metres or more above the ground, so they can't hold in the air next to it. What they stop is radiation escaping.

It's also wrong to say that cold "comes down" from a clear sky: cold isn't something that flows. The ground simply loses energy faster when less infrared comes back to it. And clouds aren't a heat source like a radiator: the infrared they send down depends on their own temperature, which is kept up largely by absorbing infrared from below.

title: Melting Arctic ice

figure.alt: Parallel rays of sunlight fall on a floe of sea ice on the left and on open ocean on the right.

question: As Arctic sea ice melts in summer, it exposes the much darker open ocean underneath. Assume the sunlight reaching the surface stays the same. Does this change make the Arctic warm faster, slower, or make no difference?
options: Faster
Slower
No difference
It depends only on the amount of carbon dioxide
reveal:
Faster. The fraction of incoming sunlight that a surface reflects is its albedo. Sea ice has an albedo of about 0.5–0.7; open ocean, about 0.06. So the ocean absorbs most of the sunlight that the ice would have reflected.

For example, with sunlight of 300 $\text{W m}^{-2}$ reaching the surface, a square metre of sea ice with an albedo of 0.60 absorbs $(1 - 0.60) \times 300 = 120$ W, while a square metre of open ocean absorbs $(1 - 0.06) \times 300 \approx 280$ W: more than twice as much.

The extra energy warms the water, which melts more ice from below and at its edges, exposing even more dark water. A change that causes more of the same change is a positive feedback, here the ice–albedo feedback. It is one of the reasons the Arctic is warming several times faster than the world as a whole.

revealFigure.alt: On the sea ice, a thick arrow of sunlight comes in, a slightly thinner arrow labelled 60 percent reflected goes back up, and a small arrow labelled 40 percent absorbed goes into the ice. On the open ocean, a tiny arrow labelled 6 percent reflected goes back up and a thick arrow labelled 94 percent absorbed goes into the water.
revealFigure.caption: Arrow widths show roughly how much of the sunlight is reflected and absorbed, for sea ice with an albedo of 0.60.

tempting:
"Slower" is tempting because melting ice takes in energy (latent heat) without getting warmer, which holds the temperature near 0 °C while it melts. But that energy came from absorbed sunlight in the first place, and once the ice has gone, the dark water absorbs far more sunlight than the ice did.

"It depends only on the amount of carbon dioxide" treats greenhouse gases as the only control on temperature. They affect how much infrared escapes to space; albedo affects how much sunlight is absorbed in the first place. Both are part of the energy balance. "No difference" misses that ice and water at the same temperature can absorb very different fractions of the sunlight.

title: Helium or argon?

figure.alt: Two identical large syringes, each sealed at the nozzle with a piston that can slide freely. The top one holds 1 g of helium and the bottom one 1 g of argon. Both pistons are drawn at the same place, with a double-headed arrow and a question mark showing that their final positions are unknown.
figure.caption: The pistons are drawn in the same place only to show the syringes; they can slide freely. Where do they settle? (Not to scale.)

question: Two identical, extra-large syringes are sealed at the nozzle, and each piston can slide freely without friction. One syringe holds 1 g of helium and the other holds 1 g of argon. Both gases are at room temperature and atmospheric pressure, and both behave as ideal gases. Which gas takes up the larger volume?
options: The helium, about 10 times as much
The argon, about 10 times as much
They take up the same volume
The helium, about twice as much
reveal:
The volume of an ideal gas depends on the number of particles, not on their mass. At the same pressure and temperature, $V = \dfrac{nRT}{P}$, so the volume is proportional to the amount of gas $n$.

A helium atom is about 10 times lighter than an argon atom (molar masses about 4 and 40 g $\text{mol}^{-1}$), so 1 g of helium contains about 10 times as many atoms. At 20 °C (293 K) and $1.0 \times 10^5$ Pa:

  • Helium: $n = \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25$ mol, so $V = \dfrac{0.25 \times 8.31 \times 293}{1.0 \times 10^5} = 6.1 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$, about 6 litres.
  • Argon: $n = \dfrac{1}{40} = 0.025$ mol, so $V = 6.1 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^3$, about 0.6 litres.

Each piston settles where the pressure of the gas equals atmospheric pressure. The heavier argon atoms move more slowly, but at the same temperature every atom has the same average kinetic energy, $\tfrac{3}{2}k_BT$, so each atom contributes the same share of the pressure whatever gas it belongs to.

revealFigure.alt: The same two syringes after the pistons have settled. The helium fills most of its syringe, labelled 6.1 litres; the argon fills a short section near the nozzle, labelled 0.61 litres.
revealFigure.caption: Where the pistons settle: about 6.1 L of helium and 0.61 L of argon.

tempting:
"Same mass, same amount of gas" feels natural, because for solids and liquids we usually measure an amount by its mass. But for a gas at a given temperature and pressure, the volume depends on the number of particles. Lighter atoms mean more atoms in each gram, so more volume. (This is Avogadro's idea: equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of particles.)

"About twice as much" tempts people who know that helium is lighter but guess the factor instead of working it out from the molar masses: 40 ÷ 4 = 10.

title: A balloon in the freezer

figure.alt: A sealed, blown-up balloon at 20 °C, with an arrow pointing to an upright freezer at −18 °C. The freezer door is open and a question mark is drawn inside it.

question: A sealed balloon is taken from a room at 20 °C and put in a freezer at −18 °C. Treat the air inside as an ideal gas, and assume its pressure stays the same (ignore any change in the stretch of the rubber). Once the air in the balloon has cooled to −18 °C, what has happened to the balloon's volume?
options: It stays the same size
It shrinks by about 13%
It shrinks to about half
It shrinks to almost nothing
reveal:
At constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of ideal gas is proportional to its kelvin temperature (Charles's law): $\dfrac{V}{T} = \text{constant}$.

$T_1 = 20 + 273 = 293$ K and $T_2 = -18 + 273 = 255$ K, so $\dfrac{V_2}{V_1} = \dfrac{255}{293} = 0.87$.

The balloon shrinks to 87% of its original volume, a drop of about 13%. That's a noticeable change, but nowhere near empty. Take it out and let it warm up again, and it goes back to its original size.
tempting:
In degrees Celsius the temperature goes from +20 to −18, which sounds like going "below nothing", so it is tempting to think the gas must shrink to half or to almost nothing. But 0 °C is just the melting point of ice, not a zero of anything in the gas. At −18 °C the molecules still have plenty of kinetic energy. What matters is the change compared with absolute zero: a drop of 38 K from 293 K.

Others think a sealed balloon can't change size because no air gets in or out. The mass of air is fixed, but its volume isn't.

title: The freezer door that sticks

figure.alt: An upright freezer at minus 18 degrees Celsius in a room at 20 degrees Celsius. Its door has just been closed, and a hand is pulling the handle to open it again.
figure.caption: Opened, closed, and pulled again a few seconds later. Not to scale.

question: An upright freezer keeps its inside at −18 °C in a kitchen at 20 °C. You open the door for a few seconds, take something out, and close it. A few seconds later you try to open it again, and it is noticeably harder to pull open than it was the first time. If you wait a minute or two, it opens easily again. What causes the door to stick?
options: The cold makes the rubber seal stiffer, so it grips the door
The air inside shrinks and sucks the door inwards
The warm air that got in cools quickly, so its pressure falls below the pressure outside
Water vapour on the seal freezes and glues the door shut
reveal:
The warm air that got in cools quickly, so its pressure falls below the pressure of the room air outside.

While the door is open, the cold air spills out (it is denser) and room air at about 20 °C, or 293 K, takes its place. When the door shuts, that air is trapped in a fixed volume and the cold walls and shelves cool it quickly towards −18 °C, or 255 K. For a fixed amount of gas at constant volume, pressure is proportional to absolute temperature ($\dfrac{p}{T}$ constant), so the pressure inside falls from about 100 kPa to $100 \times \dfrac{255}{293} = 87$ kPa. The pressure outside is still 100 kPa, so there is a net inward pressure of about 13 kPa on the door.

Pressure is force per unit area, $p = \dfrac{F}{A}$. For a door 0.5 m by 1.2 m, area 0.6 $\text{m}^2$, the net inward force would be $F = pA = 13 \times 10^3 \times 0.6 = 7.8 \times 10^3$ N, the weight of about 800 kg! In practice the force is much smaller, because the seal is not perfectly airtight: air starts leaking back in at once, the air inside does not all cool to −18 °C in a few seconds, and the door and seal flex inwards a little, which reduces the volume and so the pressure drop. Even so, the extra force needed is easy to feel.

Air keeps seeping in through the seal until the pressure inside equals the pressure outside, which takes a minute or so, and the door opens freely again. Some freezers have a small one-way vent for exactly this reason.
tempting:
"The air inside shrinks and sucks the door inwards" has the right idea about the air cooling, but the wrong picture of forces. A gas cannot pull on anything: its molecules only push when they hit a surface. The air inside pushes outwards on the door with a lower pressure than before, and the room air pushes inwards with its full pressure. It is the outside air that holds the door shut. Also the air does not "shrink": the volume is fixed by the cabinet, so it is the pressure that falls.

"The seal gets stiffer" and "water vapour freezes the door shut" both fail the timing test. The seal was just as cold the first time you opened the door, and ice would take much longer than a few seconds to form and would not vanish again a minute later. The sticking appears quickly and disappears quickly, exactly like a pressure difference that air leaking through the seal slowly removes.

title: At what temperature does water boil?

figure.alt: Three pans of water being heated: one on a flat mountain summit 3000 m up, one on a stove at sea level beside the waves, and one in a pressure cooker with a locked lid and a valve. Each has a thermometer whose reading is hidden behind a question mark.
figure.caption: Three pans of water, all being heated. The thermometer readings are hidden. Not to scale.

question: Three pans of water are heated until they boil: one on a camping stove 3000 m up a mountain, one in a kitchen at sea level, and one inside a pressure cooker with its lid locked on. Before you look at any thermometer, answer the question in the title: at what temperature does water boil? Give a number if you can, and a reason.
reveal:
There is no single answer: water boils at whatever temperature matches the pressure on it. 100 °C is the boiling point at normal atmospheric pressure, about 101 kPa, and nowhere else.

Boiling is different from evaporation. Evaporation happens only at the surface, at any temperature. Boiling happens when bubbles of water vapour can form and grow inside the liquid. A bubble can only grow if the vapour inside it pushes outwards at least as hard as the surroundings push in. The pressure a liquid's own vapour can exert (its vapour pressure, beyond the course) rises steeply with temperature, so water boils at the temperature where its vapour pressure reaches the pressure acting on it.

That is why the three pans give three different readings. At sea level the air pushes down with about 101 kPa and water boils at 100 °C. At 3000 m the air pressure is only about 70 kPa, so the vapour wins at about 90 °C: the water boils earlier, and because it never gets hotter than 90 °C, pasta and potatoes cook slowly. In the pressure cooker the trapped steam raises the pressure to roughly 200 kPa (twice atmospheric), and the water does not boil until about 120 °C, so food cooks faster. Go the other way and put a glass of room-temperature water in a vacuum chamber: once the pressure drops to about 2.3 kPa the water boils at 20 °C, without getting any warmer.

Whatever the boiling temperature, boiling still needs energy. While the water boils, the energy supplied goes into the specific latent heat of vaporization, $Q = mL$, not into raising the temperature: the thermometer stays put until the water has gone.

One more twist, a real hazard: water heated in a microwave in a smooth, clean cup can go above 100 °C without boiling, because a bubble needs a rough spot, a scratch or a speck of dust to start on (a nucleation site, beyond the course). The water is then superheated. Dropping in a spoon or a teabag gives the bubbles their start, and the water can erupt out of the cup all at once and scald you. Heating water in a microwave with a wooden stirrer or a scratched mug in it avoids this.
tempting:
"100 °C" is the answer almost everyone gives, because it is the number we all learn. It is true only at one pressure, about 101 kPa. Mountaineers, pressure-cooker users and vacuum-chamber users all see water boiling at other temperatures.

"When it reaches its boiling point" sounds safe but explains nothing: it just renames the question. The physics is the match between the water's vapour pressure and the pressure on it.

"When bubbles appear" is a tempting test, but the first small bubbles on the bottom of a pan are dissolved air coming out of solution, well before boiling. The rolling bubbles of boiling are made of water vapour, and they form throughout the liquid.

title: Why does the smell take so long?

figure.alt: A room seen from the side. At the left, an open perfume bottle stands on a small table with its stopper beside it. At the right, 5 metres away, a person stands and smells nothing yet. The air is still.
figure.caption: The bottle is opened at one end of a still room; the person is 5 m away. Not to scale.

question: A perfume bottle is opened at one end of a room 5 m long. The air is completely still: no draughts, no heating, nobody moving (an idealised room: ignore even the warmth of the person's body). At room temperature the perfume molecules that leave the bottle are moving at a few hundred metres per second (around 200 to 300 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ for a fairly heavy molecule; the air molecules around them average about 500 $\text{m s}^{-1}$). At that speed a molecule could cross the room in a few hundredths of a second. Yet a person at the far end smells nothing for a very long time. Why?
options: The molecules slow down to walking pace as soon as they leave the bottle
They collide with air molecules billions of times a second and zigzag, so they get nowhere fast
Smell travels through the air as a wave, and that wave moves much more slowly than the molecules do
Perfume molecules are heavier than air molecules, so they sink to the floor before they can spread out
reveal:
They zigzag. The molecules really are moving at hundreds of metres per second, but they cannot travel in a straight line for more than a tiny fraction of a millimetre before hitting an air molecule and heading off in a new direction.

In the kinetic model of a gas, the molecules fly about in straight lines between collisions, and their average kinetic energy is set by the temperature: $\overline{E_k} = \tfrac{3}{2}k_BT$. At 20 °C that gives a perfume molecule of molar mass around 150 g $\text{mol}^{-1}$ a typical speed of about 220 $\text{m s}^{-1}$, and a nitrogen molecule about 510 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. Nothing slows them down: as long as the room stays at 20 °C, they keep these speeds for ever. The same collisions that give a gas its pressure also get in the way of travel. At atmospheric pressure a molecule travels on average only about $7 \times 10^{-8}$ m, a few hundred molecular diameters, before hitting another one, so a perfume molecule moving at 220 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ is knocked off course about $\dfrac{220}{7 \times 10^{-8}} \approx 3 \times 10^9$ times every second.

Each collision sends the molecule off in a fresh, effectively random direction, so its path is a random walk. A random walk has a famous property (beyond the course, so take it as a stated result): after $N$ steps of length $\lambda$ the walker typically ends up only about $\sqrt{N}\,\lambda$ from the start, not $N\lambda$, because the steps so often cancel each other out. With about $3 \times 10^9$ steps of $7 \times 10^{-8}$ m in one second, $\sqrt{N}\,\lambda \approx 5.5 \times 10^4 \times 7 \times 10^{-8} \approx 4 \times 10^{-3}$ m: about 4 mm of net progress for roughly 220 m of actual travel. To get about 1000 times further, to 5 m, needs about a million times as many steps, roughly $10^6$ s, which is nearly two weeks. That is diffusion, and it really is that slow over room-sized distances.

So in a real room the smell arrives by a different route: the air itself moves. Convection currents from warm bodies, radiators and sunlit walls, and the wake of anyone walking past, carry the vapour-laden air across the room in seconds or minutes, and diffusion only finishes the job over the last few millimetres, into your nose.

revealFigure.alt: A jagged path of 60 straight steps of equal length in random directions, starting at a blue dot and ending at an orange dot. A dashed straight line joins the start to the end; it is much shorter than the path.
revealFigure.caption: A random walk of 60 equal steps in computed random directions. The walker ends only about 8 step lengths from the start ($\sqrt{60} \approx 7.7$), a typical result, after walking 60 step lengths to get there. A perfume molecule makes thousands of millions of such steps every second, each about $7 \times 10^{-8}$ m long.

tempting:
"They slow down to walking pace" is the most natural guess, because the smell does spread at about walking pace. But a molecule's speed is fixed by the temperature of the gas it is in, and the room is no cooler than the bottle. The molecules never slow down; they just keep being turned round.

"Smell is a wave" confuses two very different things that travel through air. A sound wave is a disturbance that passes from molecule to molecule, so it travels at 340 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ while each molecule only jiggles about its own position. A smell is the molecules themselves arriving at your nose; nothing arrives until they do.

"They are heavier, so they sink" sounds like common sense, but in a gas the constant collisions mix everything far faster than gravity can sort it. Carbon dioxide is heavier than nitrogen, yet the air in a room does not separate into layers, and you can smell perfume at nose height, not just at your feet. (Over kilometres of height the atmosphere does thin out, but it stays well mixed.)

title: Cooling the cabin air

figure.alt: An airliner in flight, with the outside air at −50 °C. A duct runs from one of its engines up into the passenger cabin.
figure.caption: The duct carries compressed outside air from the engine to the cabin.

question: At cruising height, the air outside an airliner is about −50 °C. The air for the cabin is taken from outside and squeezed by the engines' compressors to a much higher pressure. Yet before it can be used in the cabin, this air has to be cooled, not heated. Why?
reveal:
Compressing a gas means doing work on it, and if the compression is fast, that work raises its temperature.

Inside the engine the air is squeezed in a tiny fraction of a second, far too quickly for much thermal energy to flow out through the walls. So the compression is close to adiabatic: $Q \approx 0$. In the first law, $Q = \Delta U + W$, where $W$ is the work done by the gas, this gives $\Delta U = -W$. In a compression, work is done on the gas, so $W$ is negative and $\Delta U$ is positive: the internal energy of the air rises, and so does its temperature.

The compressors squeeze the air to many times its starting pressure, so it comes out far hotter than the cabin needs, hotter than boiling water. Cooling units bring it down to a comfortable temperature before it reaches the passengers. You can feel the same effect on a small scale: the barrel of a bicycle pump gets warm when you pump hard.
tempting: It is tempting to think "the air starts at −50 °C, so it must still be cold", or that only heating can raise a temperature. But the temperature of a gas rises whenever its internal energy rises, and doing work on it is just as good a way of increasing internal energy as heating it. In an adiabatic compression, all the work done on the gas goes into its internal energy.

title: The open fridge

figure.alt: A small kitchen with the window and door shut. A fridge plugged into the wall stands with its door wide open. A thermometer on the wall has a question mark beside it.

question: On a hot day, someone shuts the door and window of a small kitchen and leaves the fridge door wide open, hoping to cool the room down. The fridge keeps running. Assume the kitchen is well insulated, so no thermal energy passes through the walls, window or door; the fridge's electricity still comes in through the wall socket. The fridge is nearly empty. What happens to the temperature of the kitchen over the next few hours?
options: It falls
It rises
It stays the same
It falls at first, then stays steady
reveal:
The kitchen gets warmer. A fridge doesn't make "cold": it is a pump that moves thermal energy. It takes thermal energy from the inside of the cabinet and releases it, together with the energy it takes from the electricity supply, from the warm coils at the back.

With the door open, the inside of the fridge is part of the kitchen. The thermal energy it removes from the air in front of it is released back into the same kitchen from the coils behind it, so that part just goes round in a loop. But the fridge also takes electrical energy all the time it runs, and all of that ends up in the kitchen too.

Take the whole kitchen as the system. No thermal energy crosses the walls, but the electricity supply keeps transferring energy in, so by the first law (conservation of energy) the internal energy of the kitchen rises, and so does its temperature. A fridge running non-stop at about 150 W adds over 0.5 MJ every hour. Just in front of the door it may feel cool for a few minutes, as the cold air and food from inside mix with the room, but the steady energy input soon wins.
tempting:
We think of a fridge as something that "makes cold", so it seems that opening it should cool the room. But a fridge only makes one place colder by making another place warmer, and it needs an energy input to do it. When both places are in the same closed room, the only overall effect is that energy input, which warms the room. This is why an air-conditioner has to release its thermal energy outside the building.

"It stays the same" is tempting once you see that the fridge just moves thermal energy from the front of the kitchen to the back. That part does cancel out, but it forgets the electrical energy the fridge takes in all the time, which also ends up in the kitchen. "It falls at first, then stays steady" comes from the cool air you feel just in front of the open door for the first few minutes: that cool air soon mixes with the rest of the room, and from then on the energy input warms the whole kitchen.

title: Swapping the lamps

figure.alt: Two circuit diagrams. Before: a cell in series with lamp A and then lamp B, with A nearer the positive terminal. After: the same circuit with the two lamps swapped, so B is nearer the positive terminal.
figure.caption: Lamps A and B are different. Only their positions change.

question: A cell is connected in series with two different filament lamps, A and B, with lamp A nearer the positive terminal. The two lamps are then swapped round, so that lamp B is nearer the positive terminal. What happens?
options: Lamp A becomes brighter
Lamp B becomes brighter
Nothing changes
Both lamps become dimmer
reveal:
Nothing changes. A series circuit has only one path, and charge can't pile up anywhere or be used up, so the current is the same at every point in the loop. The same current flows through A as through B, whichever comes first.

The total resistance hasn't changed, so the current is the same as before. The power dissipated in each lamp is $P = I^2R$, and each lamp still has its own resistance, so each lamp is exactly as bright as it was. If A was the brighter lamp before the swap, it still is.
tempting:
Many people picture current as something that gets "used up" by each lamp, so the lamp that gets the current first should get the most. But the lamps don't use up charge: they transfer energy from the moving charges. Charge flows round the whole loop at the same rate everywhere, and all the charges start moving together as soon as the circuit is complete.

The two lamps can be different in brightness, but that is because they have different resistances, not because of where they are in the loop.

title: The wire across the lamp

figure.alt: Three lamps, numbered 1, 2 and 3, connected in a row in series with a battery. A wire is connected from one side of lamp 2 to the other side, so that it bypasses the lamp.
figure.caption: The wire added joins the two sides of lamp 2.

question: Three identical lamps are connected in series with a battery, and all three glow. The battery's internal resistance is negligible, and you can treat the resistance of each lamp as constant. A thick copper wire is now connected across lamp 2, from one side of it to the other, as shown. What happens to lamps 1 and 3?
options: They both go out
They glow as before
They glow more brightly
They glow more dimly
reveal:
They glow more brightly, and lamp 2 goes out.

The copper wire has almost no resistance, so it is a short circuit across lamp 2: nearly all the current flows through the wire instead of the lamp, and the potential difference across the lamp (and the wire) is almost zero. With no p.d. across it, lamp 2 goes out.

For lamps 1 and 3, what matters is the total resistance of the circuit. Call the battery's emf $\varepsilon$ and each lamp's resistance $R$. Before, the current was $I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{3R}$. With lamp 2 bypassed, the total resistance is $2R$, so $I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{2R}$: the current is 1.5 times larger. The power in each remaining lamp, $P = I^2 R$, is $1.5^2 = 2.25$ times larger, so they glow much more brightly.

(A real filament's resistance rises as it gets hotter, so the increase is a little less than 2.25 times, but the lamps still get brighter. A short circuit across the battery would be a different story: a very large current and a hot, damaged battery.)
tempting:
"They both go out" comes from thinking of a short circuit as something that stops the whole circuit working. It only short-circuits the part it is connected across; the rest of the loop is still complete, with a lower total resistance than before.

"They glow more dimly" comes from thinking that the new wire "takes" current away from the other lamps, or that the current is used up. In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere, and its size is set by the whole circuit: less resistance means more current, for every component.

"They glow as before" would be right if the lamps were in parallel, each with the full battery p.d. across it. In series, every lamp's share of the p.d. depends on the others.

title: 60 W or 100 W?

figure.alt: A circuit diagram: a 60 W lamp and a 100 W lamp connected in series to a 230 V supply.
figure.caption: Both lamps are designed for 230 V.

question: Two old-style filament lamps are both designed for the 230 V mains: one is rated 60 W and the other 100 W. They are connected in series to a 230 V supply. Assume each lamp's resistance stays the same as when it works normally at its rating, and that the lamp dissipating more power glows more brightly. Which lamp glows more brightly?
options: The 60 W lamp
The 100 W lamp
They are equally bright
Neither lights
reveal:
A lamp's rating is the power it dissipates with 230 V across it. From $P = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$, each lamp's resistance is $R = \dfrac{V^2}{P}$:

  • 60 W lamp: $R = \dfrac{230^2}{60} = 882\ \Omega$
  • 100 W lamp: $R = \dfrac{230^2}{100} = 529\ \Omega$

So the lower-rated lamp has the higher resistance. In series, both lamps carry the same current: $I = \dfrac{230}{882 + 529} = 0.163$ A. Then $P = I^2R$ gives about 23 W for the 60 W lamp and 14 W for the 100 W lamp. The 60 W lamp glows more brightly, although both are much dimmer than normal.

In reality a filament's resistance is lower when it is cooler, so both resistances are smaller than these values. The 100 W lamp runs further below its normal temperature, so its resistance drops more, and if anything the 60 W lamp wins by even more.
tempting: "The 100 W lamp is brighter" is true when each lamp has the full 230 V across it, as at home, where lamps are connected in parallel. Then $P = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$ applies with the same $V$, and the lower resistance wins. In series it is the current that is the same for both, so $P = I^2R$ shows that the higher resistance wins. A power rating describes a lamp under its rated conditions, not in every circuit.

title: High voltage, low current?

figure.alt: Two electricity pylons carrying cables labelled 400 kV, with a line running on to a small building labelled to users.
figure.caption: The 400 kV is the potential difference between the lines (roughly, between a line and the ground). Not to scale.

question: The cables on the big pylons that cross the countryside are at a potential difference of about 400 kV from the ground, yet the current in them is only a few hundred amperes. A student objects: "$V = IR$, so a very high voltage must mean a very high current." The current is not very high. What is wrong with the student's reasoning?
options: Nothing: the current in a 400 kV cable really is enormous
The 400 kV is not the p.d. across the cable's resistance, so putting it into V = IR gives the wrong current
V = IR does not apply to power lines because they carry alternating current
The cable's resistance is so large that it cancels the high voltage
reveal:
The 400 kV is not the potential difference across the cable's resistance. It is the p.d. between the line and the ground (or between two lines). The p.d. that drives current along the cable is the small difference between the potentials at its two ends, and that is what $V = IR$ links to the current: $V_{\text{cable}} = IR_{\text{cable}}$, which is only a few kilovolts.

The current is fixed by the power being delivered, not by the line voltage alone: $P = IV$, so $I = \dfrac{P}{V}$. For 100 MW sent at 400 kV, $I = \dfrac{100 \times 10^6}{400 \times 10^3} = 250$ A. If the cable's resistance is 5 Ω, the p.d. along the cable is $V = IR = 250 \times 5 = 1250$ V, about 1.25 kV out of 400 kV, and the power wasted as heat in the cable is $P = I^2 R = 250^2 \times 5 = 3.1 \times 10^5$ W, about 0.31 MW, which is 0.3% of the power sent.

Now send the same 100 MW at 40 kV. The current is ten times larger, $I = \dfrac{100 \times 10^6}{40 \times 10^3} = 2500$ A, the p.d. along the cable is $2500 \times 5 = 12.5$ kV, and the loss is $I^2 R = 2500^2 \times 5 = 3.1 \times 10^7$ W, about 31 MW: nearly a third of the power is lost before it arrives. So for a given power, a high transmission voltage means a low current and small $I^2 R$ losses. That is exactly why the grid uses such high voltages (and transformers to step them up and back down).
tempting:
"The current really is enormous" follows directly from the student's slip. $V = IR$ is correct, but $V$ must be the p.d. across the resistance you are using. The 400 kV is the p.d. between the cable and the ground: across the whole route from the line, through the users' appliances and back to earth. $V = IR$ with that route's resistance (about 1600 Ω here) gives the 250 A correctly. Pairing the 400 kV with the cable's own 5 Ω instead would predict 80 000 A, and that is the student's mistake.

"The cable's resistance is huge" tries to rescue $V = IR$ by making $R$ large, but transmission cables are thick aluminium and steel with a resistance of only a few ohms over many kilometres, deliberately kept low. A huge resistance would waste enormous power as $I^2 R$ heating.

"It does not apply to alternating current" is an excuse rather than an explanation. For a resistor, $V = IR$ holds at every instant whichever way the current flows; the student's error is about which p.d. to use, not about a.c.

title: The bouncing ball

figure.alt: A ball above a hard floor, with a dashed outline of the same ball touching the floor and a double-headed arrow showing that it moves up and down between the two positions.
figure.caption: The ball bounces back to the same height every time.

question: A ball is dropped onto a hard floor. Assume it bounces perfectly, losing no energy, and that air resistance is negligible. It bounces up and down to the same height again and again, and each bounce takes the same time. Is its motion simple harmonic motion?
options: Yes: it repeats with a fixed period, and that's all SHM needs
Yes: gravity always pulls it back down towards the floor
No: its acceleration isn't proportional to its displacement from a fixed point
No: SHM has to be a side-to-side motion, like a pendulum
reveal:
No. SHM needs a particular kind of force: the acceleration must be proportional to the displacement from the equilibrium position and directed back towards it, $a = -\omega^2 x$. The further the object is from equilibrium, the harder it is pulled back.

The ball isn't like that. In the air its acceleration is $g$ downwards whether it is 1 cm or 1 m above the floor; then, during its very short contact with the floor, it has a huge upward acceleration. Its graph of height against time is a chain of parabolas with sharp corners at each bounce, not a smooth sine curve.

There's a quick test, too. In SHM the period doesn't depend on the amplitude. The ball's does: it takes $\sqrt{2h/g}$ to fall a height $h$ and the same time to rise again, so dropped from 1.0 m each bounce takes 0.90 s, but dropped from 0.25 m it takes only 0.45 s. A quarter of the height gives half the period.

revealFigure.alt: Two graphs against time. The top graph, height of the bouncing ball, is a row of upside-down parabolas that meet the time axis in sharp points. The bottom graph, displacement in SHM, is a smooth sine-shaped curve with the same period.
revealFigure.caption: Top: height of the bouncing ball against time, parabolas joined by sharp corners. Bottom: displacement of an object in SHM against time, a smooth sine curve with the same period.

tempting:
Every SHM is periodic, but not every periodic motion is SHM: a bouncing ball, a heartbeat and a clock's hands all repeat. What makes SHM special is a restoring force that grows in proportion to the displacement.

Gravity does always pull the ball down, but by the same amount at every height, so it isn't a restoring force of the SHM kind. And SHM doesn't have to be side to side: a mass on a spring moves up and down in SHM.

title: Half a spring

figure.alt: Left: a mass m hanging from a long spring, labelled T = 0.80 s, whole spring. Right: the same mass m hanging from a spring half as long, labelled T = ?, half the spring.

question: A mass hangs from a light, uniform spring and oscillates up and down with a period of 0.80 s. The spring is cut exactly in half, and the same mass is hung from one of the halves and set oscillating. The spring obeys Hooke's law throughout. What is the new period?
reveal:
The key is what happens to the spring constant. Hang a weight from the whole spring and every coil stretches a little. Hang the same weight from half the spring and each coil stretches by the same amount as before, but there are only half as many coils, so the total extension is halved. Half the extension for the same force means the spring constant has doubled: the half spring is twice as stiff.

For a mass–spring system, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$. With $m$ unchanged and $k$ doubled, $T$ is divided by $\sqrt{2}$:

$T = \dfrac{0.80}{\sqrt{2}} = 0.57$ s
tempting: "Half the spring, half the period" (0.40 s) forgets the square root: $T$ depends on $\sqrt{k}$, not on $k$. "Still 0.80 s" treats the spring constant as a fixed property of the material, like density, but it depends on the spring's length too. And 1.1 s comes from thinking a shorter spring is weaker. It is actually stiffer: it's harder to stretch a short piece of spring by 1 cm than a long one.

title: Two clocks on the Moon

figure.alt: Two clocks standing side by side on the lunar surface, with the Earth small in the sky. The left clock is driven by a swinging pendulum; the right clock is driven by a mass bouncing on a spring.
figure.caption: The pendulum clock and the mass-on-a-spring clock, taken to the Moon, where $g \approx 1.6$ $\text{m s}^{-2}$. Not to scale.

question: Two clocks keep perfect time on Earth. One is regulated by a swinging pendulum; the other by a mass bouncing up and down on a spring. Both are taken to the Moon, where the gravitational field strength is about 1.6 $\text{m s}^{-2}$ instead of 9.8 $\text{m s}^{-2}$, and set going again. Both oscillate with small amplitudes, and friction and air resistance are negligible. What happens to their timekeeping?
options: Both clocks run slow
The pendulum clock runs slow; the spring clock keeps time
The spring clock runs slow; the pendulum clock keeps time
Both clocks keep time
reveal:
The pendulum clock runs slow; the spring clock keeps perfect time.

The period of a simple pendulum is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$: it depends on $g$ because gravity provides the restoring force. With $g$ smaller, each swing takes longer, by a factor $\sqrt{\dfrac{9.8}{1.6}} = 2.5$. A pendulum that swung once a second on Earth now takes about 2.5 s, so the clock shows only about 24 minutes for every real hour.

The period of a mass on a spring is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$: no $g$ at all. The restoring force comes from the spring, and the mass $m$ (the inertia of the oscillating object) and the spring constant $k$ are the same on the Moon as on Earth. The spring does sag less: the equilibrium extension is $\dfrac{mg}{k}$, so on the Moon the mass hangs at about a sixth of its Earth extension ($\dfrac{1.6}{9.8} = 0.16$). But the mass oscillates about that new equilibrium position with exactly the same period, so the clock keeps time.

This is why a pendulum can be used to measure $g$, while a spring-driven balance wheel (the heart of a mechanical wristwatch) does not care where it is.
tempting:
"Both run slow, because everything is lighter on the Moon" mixes up weight and mass. Weight (the force $mg$) is smaller on the Moon, but mass, the inertia that resists acceleration, is not. The spring's restoring force depends on its extension, not on gravity, and the mass it has to accelerate is unchanged, so the spring oscillation is unchanged.

"The spring clock runs slow because the mass hangs lower on the Moon" gets the sag backwards (it hangs higher, because its weight is smaller) and, more importantly, confuses the equilibrium position with the period. Shifting where the mass hangs does not change how quickly it bounces about that point.

"Both keep time" is tempting if you think a pendulum is just another oscillator with a fixed length. But its restoring force is the component of the weight along the swing, and a smaller weight means a smaller force, a smaller acceleration and a longer period.

title: The ant on the loudspeaker

figure.alt: A loudspeaker lies on its back on a bench with its cone facing upwards, drawn in section as a shallow V. An ant stands on the sloping cone. A blue double-headed arrow beside the cone shows that it moves up and down.
figure.caption: The cone moves straight up and down. The ant is not to scale.

question: A loudspeaker lies on its back so that its cone moves vertically. An ant stands on the cone. The cone moves up and down in simple harmonic motion with an amplitude of 2.0 mm, and the frequency is turned up slowly from a very low value. The ant does not grip the cone or jump; it just stands there, and the cone can push on it but not pull. Take $g = 9.8$ $\text{m s}^{-2}$. What happens?
options: The ant stays in contact with the cone however high the frequency goes
Once the frequency passes a certain value, the ant loses contact at the bottom of each oscillation
Once the frequency passes a certain value, the ant loses contact at the top of each oscillation
Whether the ant loses contact depends on its mass
reveal:
At the top, once the frequency passes about 11 Hz, whatever the ant's mass.

In simple harmonic motion the acceleration is proportional to the displacement and directed towards the equilibrium position: $a = -\omega^2 x$. So the cone's acceleration is largest at the two ends of its travel, where it is $\omega^2 A$ in size, and at the top it points downwards: the cone is being yanked back down towards the middle.

Now think about the ant. Only two forces act on it: its weight $mg$ downwards and the normal force $N$ from the cone upwards. The cone can push the ant up but cannot pull it down, so $N$ can never be negative. The ant's largest possible downward acceleration is therefore $g$, when $N = 0$ and it is in free fall. As long as the cone's downward acceleration at the top, $\omega^2 A$, is less than $g$, the cone just pushes a little less hard ($N = m(g - \omega^2 A)$) and the ant follows it down. But once $\omega^2 A > g$ the cone drops away faster than the ant can fall, and they separate at the top.

The condition $\omega^2 A = g$ gives $\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{g}{A}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{9.8}{0.0020}} = \sqrt{4900} = 70$ $\text{rad s}^{-1}$, so $f = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi} = \dfrac{70}{2\pi} = 11.1$ Hz. The mass cancelled, so a heavy beetle would lose contact at exactly the same frequency as the ant. With a smaller amplitude the frequency needed is higher ($f \propto 1/\sqrt{A}$): at 0.50 mm it would be 22 Hz. The same idea explains why a coin left on a rattling washing machine starts to dance, and why loose grit on a vibrating table hops into the air.

revealFigure.alt: A graph of the cone's displacement against time: a smooth sine curve between plus A and minus A. One peak is marked with a dot labelled top, ant leaves here, with an orange arrow pointing downwards from it labelled acceleration of cone.
revealFigure.caption: The cone's displacement against time (a computed sine curve). At the top, the cone's acceleration is downwards and of size $\omega^2 A$; the ant cannot accelerate downwards faster than $g$, so it is left behind when $\omega^2 A > g$.

tempting:
"At the bottom" is tempting because the bottom is where the motion feels most violent: the cone is accelerating upwards hardest there, and the normal force on the ant is at its largest, $N = m(g + \omega^2 A)$. The ant feels heaviest at the bottom, but a big push upwards is the opposite of losing contact. Contact is lost where the normal force falls to zero, and that is the top.

"It depends on the mass" comes from thinking a heavier ant is harder to throw off. But both its weight and the force needed to accelerate it are proportional to its mass, so $m$ cancels: the only question is whether the cone's acceleration exceeds $g$. A grain of sand and a coin leave at the same frequency.

"Never loses contact" assumes the cone can always take the ant with it. Going up, it can: it pushes. Coming down from the top, it can only let the ant fall, and nothing can make the ant fall faster than $g$.

title: Where is purple?

figure.alt: The visible spectrum as a coloured strip from violet at 400 nanometres, through blue, green, yellow and orange, to red at 700 nanometres. Below it is an empty dashed box labelled 'purple?'.
figure.caption: The visible spectrum, from violet (about 400 nm) to red (about 700 nm). The reddish purples and magentas aren't in it.

question: The visible spectrum runs from violet (about 400 nm), through blue, green, yellow and orange, to red (about 700 nm). Violet can look a little purplish, but the reddish purples and magentas, the colours between red and violet on a colour wheel, aren't anywhere in the spectrum. Yet we clearly see them. Where does purple come from?
options: Purple light has a wavelength just shorter than violet, in the ultraviolet
We see purple when red light and blue light reach the eye together, with little green
Purple light has a wavelength between red and violet that instruments can't detect
Purple is violet light that has been made dimmer
reveal:
