In one version you add a neutron. In the other you add a proton (and an extra electron to each atom, so the atoms stay neutral). After which change would the glass still contain water?
options: Only after adding a neutron
Only after adding a proton
After either change
After neither change
reveal:
An element is defined by its proton number $Z$.

Adding a neutron changes oxygen-16, $^{16}_{\;8}\text{O}$, into oxygen-17, $^{17}_{\;8}\text{O}$: still oxygen, just a different isotope. Isotopes have the same number of electrons, so they have the same chemistry, and the glass still holds water, only slightly heavier. (Oxygen-17 is stable, and ordinary water already contains a little of it.)

Adding a proton changes $Z$ from 8 to 9, so every oxygen atom becomes fluorine-17, $^{17}_{\;9}\text{F}$. Fluorine has completely different chemistry, so the glass no longer contains water. In fact fluorine-17 is unstable: it decays by β⁺ emission with a half-life of about a minute, turning back into oxygen-17.
tempting:
"After neither change" comes from thinking that any change to a nucleus makes a new element. But changing the number of neutrons only changes the nucleon number $A$, which tells you which isotope it is, not which element.

"After either change" comes from thinking that an element's identity, or its chemistry, is decided by the electrons, which we kept balanced. But a neutral atom always has $Z$ electrons, so adding a proton (and its electron) changes how the atom bonds. And "only after adding a proton" mixes up the two particles: it is the proton, the particle that carries the charge, that sets the element.

title: The positive electroscope

figure.alt: An ultraviolet lamp shines on a zinc plate on top of a gold-leaf electroscope. Plus signs show that the plate and the leaves are positively charged, and the leaves stand apart.

question: A clean zinc plate sits on top of a gold-leaf electroscope. Ultraviolet light makes a negatively charged plate lose its charge, so the leaves fall. This time the electroscope is charged positively, so its leaves stand apart, and the same ultraviolet lamp shines on the plate. Ignore any slow leakage of charge into the air. What happens to the leaves?
options: They stay where they are
They rise further apart, because the light knocks electrons out of the plate
They fall together, because the light discharges the plate
reveal:
The leaves stay where they are. The ultraviolet photons still have more energy than zinc's work function, so photoelectrons are still released. But they leave with very little kinetic energy: for a typical ultraviolet lamp (wavelength 254 nm, photon energy 4.9 eV) and a work function of about 4.3 eV, $E_{\max} \approx 0.6$ eV.

The positive plate attracts them back. To escape, an electron would need enough energy to get away from a plate at a potential of hundreds or even thousands of volts, so every photoelectron is pulled straight back to the plate. Its charge doesn't change, so the leaves don't move.

On a negative plate the same electrons are repelled, so they leave for good and the plate discharges. The result depends on the sign of the charge because the light removes electrons, which only a negative plate has to spare.
tempting:
"They rise" is the most tempting answer, and it is half right: electrons are emitted. But emitting an electron is not the same as losing it. The pull of the positive plate is far too strong for an electron with less than 1 eV of kinetic energy to escape.

"They fall" comes from remembering that ultraviolet light discharges an electroscope without asking why. It only works when the light removes the excess charge, and only a negatively charged plate has excess electrons to lose.

title: Does the photon slow down?

figure.alt: An X-ray photon, drawn as a wavy line, travels towards an electron at rest. After the collision the electron moves off down and to the right, and the scattered photon moves off up and to the right; its path is a dashed line with a question mark.

question: In Compton scattering, an X-ray photon collides with a free electron at rest. The electron recoils, taking some of the photon's energy. Compared with the photon before the collision, how is the scattered photon different?
options: It travels more slowly
It has a longer wavelength
It has a shorter wavelength
Only its direction is different
reveal:
Its wavelength is longer. In a vacuum every photon travels at $c$, whatever its energy, so the scattered photon can't slow down. A photon's energy is set by its frequency: $E = hf = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$. Less energy means a lower frequency and so a longer wavelength.

Its momentum, $p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}$, decreases too: the electron's momentum makes up the change in the photon's momentum (as vectors), so the total momentum is conserved.

revealFigure.alt: The same collision. The scattered photon is drawn as a wavy line with a longer wavelength than the incoming photon.
revealFigure.caption: The scattered photon has a longer wavelength than the incoming photon. The change is exaggerated: for X-rays scattered through 90°, it is only about 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m.

tempting:
When a moving ball hits another ball and loses kinetic energy, it slows down, so it is natural to expect the same of a photon. But a photon's speed is fixed at $c$; what changes is its frequency and wavelength. Others link "less energy" with "shorter wavelength", but in $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$ energy and wavelength are inversely related.

"Only its direction is different" is what the wave model predicts: a wave scattered by an electron would come off with the same wavelength. Measuring the longer wavelength is exactly what made Compton scattering such strong evidence for photons.

title: Does counting speed it up?

figure.alt: Sample A: a small radioactive source in front of a Geiger–Müller tube connected to a counter showing a large number of counts. Sample B: an identical source inside a closed lead box.

question: Two identical samples of the same radioactive isotope are prepared at the same time. The half-life is 2 days. For the next 8 days, sample A sits in front of a Geiger–Müller tube that counts its decays non-stop, while sample B is shut in a thick lead box. At the end of the 8 days, how do the numbers of undecayed nuclei in the two samples compare?
options: They are the same
Fewer in A, because detecting the radiation draws out extra decays
Fewer in A, because the lead box slows down the decay of B
reveal:
They are the same (apart from random differences far too small to measure). Radioactive decay is random and spontaneous: each nucleus has a fixed chance of decaying in each second, and outside conditions such as temperature, pressure or chemical reactions have no noticeable effect on it (tiny effects have been measured only for a few unusual kinds of decay). Watching, counting, shielding or heating the sample makes no difference.

The Geiger–Müller tube only detects radiation that has already left the nuclei, and the lead only absorbs radiation that has already been emitted. After 8 days, which is 4 half-lives, both samples have $\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^4 = \tfrac{1}{16}$ of their nuclei left.

What the lead box does change is the count rate that a detector outside it would record. The activity of the source (decays per second) is the same in both.
tempting:
A detector clicking away can feel as if it is "pulling" decays out of the source. But a Geiger–Müller tube is a passive detector: it only reacts to radiation that has already been emitted.

Others imagine that a lead box "switches off" radioactivity. Lead stops the radiation getting out; it does nothing to the nuclei inside, which keep decaying at the same rate. Both mistakes mix up the count rate (what a detector records) with the activity (what the source does).

title: The overdue nucleus

figure.alt: A single nucleus, drawn as a cluster of protons and neutrons, labelled with a half-life of 10 minutes. Next to it, a stopwatch shows that 30 minutes have passed.

question: An isotope has a half-life of 10 minutes. Imagine you could watch one single nucleus of it. After 30 minutes it still hasn't decayed. What is the probability that it decays during the next 10 minutes?
options: 1 (it is certain to decay)
reveal:
The probability is $\frac{1}{2}$, exactly as it was when the stopwatch started. A nucleus doesn't age or wear out: its chance of decaying in the next 10 minutes is the same however long it has already survived. Decay is random, and a nucleus has no memory.

The half-life describes what happens to a large number of nuclei. Start with 1 000 000 of them: after 30 minutes about 125 000 are left. During the next 10 minutes about half of those, roughly 62 500, decay: the same fraction as decayed in the first 10 minutes. That is why a decay curve halves in every 10 minutes, wherever you start.

$\frac{1}{8}$ is the probability that a nucleus survives the first 30 minutes. For this nucleus that has already happened, so it no longer matters.
tempting: It feels as if a nucleus that has survived three half-lives must be "overdue", so its chance of decaying should be high ($\frac{7}{8}$) or even certain. This is the gambler's fallacy: after a coin lands heads three times in a row, the next throw is still 50:50. Others pick $\frac{1}{8}$ because they apply the fraction left after three half-lives to the nucleus's future. The half-life tells you the chance of decaying within the next half-life, counted from now, whatever has happened before.

title: Splitting iron

figure.alt: Graph of binding energy per nucleon (0 to about 9 MeV) against nucleon number A (0 to 240). The curve rises steeply for light nuclei to a broad peak marked iron-56, at about 8.8 MeV, then falls slowly to about 7.6 MeV at uranium-235, which is also marked.
figure.caption: Values for real nuclei. The three dots above the curve on the left are helium-4, carbon-12 and oxygen-16.

question: When a uranium-235 nucleus splits into two medium-sized nuclei, about 200 MeV is released. Imagine instead splitting an iron-56 nucleus into two equal halves: two aluminium-28 nuclei, each with 13 protons and 15 neutrons. Use the binding energy per nucleon curve. What would happen?
options: More energy would be released than in uranium fission
Less energy would be released than in uranium fission
No energy would be released, and none would be needed
Energy would have to be supplied
reveal:
Energy would have to be supplied. Splitting a nucleus releases energy only when the products are more tightly bound (have a higher binding energy per nucleon) than the original nucleus. Uranium-235 is on the right of the curve at about 7.6 MeV per nucleon, and its fragments sit higher, at about 8.5 MeV per nucleon, so energy is released.

Iron-56 sits at, or very close to, the top of the curve, at about 8.8 MeV per nucleon. Aluminium-28 is lower, at about 8.3 MeV per nucleon. (It lies a little below the curve, which follows the most tightly bound nucleus for each $A$; even the curve's value at $A = 28$, about 8.45 MeV, is below iron's.) So splitting iron moves down the curve:

  • binding energy of iron-56: $56 \times 8.79 \approx 492$ MeV
  • binding energy of two aluminium-28: $2 \times 28 \times 8.31 \approx 465$ MeV

The products would have about 27 MeV less binding energy, so about 27 MeV would have to be supplied, and the two products would have more mass than the iron nucleus. Iron is the end of the line both ways: joining light nuclei releases energy, and splitting very heavy nuclei releases energy, but neither works for nuclei near iron.

revealFigure.alt: Two bars compare total binding energy. Iron-56: 492 MeV. Two aluminium-28 nuclei: 27 MeV less.
revealFigure.caption: Total binding energy before and after. The products are less tightly bound, so 27 MeV would have to be supplied.

tempting:
"Splitting the atom" is famous for releasing energy, so it is tempting to think that splitting any nucleus does. Others expect a smaller nucleus to release less energy, but still some. What matters is not the size of the nucleus but which way the change goes on the binding energy per nucleon curve: fission releases energy only for nuclei much heavier than iron, whose fragments end up higher on the curve.

"No energy" assumes the top of the curve is flat. It is fairly flat for heavier nuclei, but aluminium-28 really is less tightly bound than iron-56.

title: A sphere or a sheet?

figure.alt: A solid sphere and, beside it, a thin, flat sheet.

question: Imagine a sphere of pure uranium-235 whose mass is just above the critical mass, so a chain reaction can sustain itself in it. Exactly the same uranium is then rolled out into a thin, flat sheet. Nothing surrounds either piece. Can a chain reaction still sustain itself in the sheet? Predict, then explain.
reveal:
No. A chain reaction sustains itself only if, on average, at least one neutron from each fission goes on to cause another fission. A neutron travels some distance through the uranium before it hits a nucleus, and any neutron that reaches the surface first escapes and is lost.

In the sphere, most neutrons are released far enough from the surface that enough of them cause further fissions. The sheet contains the same nuclei at the same density, but it is so thin that every fission happens close to a surface, and most neutrons escape before they can cause another fission. The chain reaction dies out.

So the critical mass depends on shape as well as material. A sphere has the smallest surface area for its volume, so it needs the least mass. Nuclear safety uses this: solutions of fissile material are kept in thin tanks and narrow pipes, shapes designed so that they cannot become critical.

revealFigure.alt: Cross-sections of the sphere and of the sheet seen edge on. From a fission at the centre of each, arrows show neutrons from fissions there travelling the same distance in different directions. In the sphere all of them stay inside; in the sheet all of them leave.
revealFigure.caption: Neutrons released by fissions at the centre (arrows show some possible directions) travel the same distance in each piece. In the sphere they are still inside the uranium; from the thin sheet they escape. Not to scale.

tempting:
It seems natural that the same amount of uranium should behave the same way whatever its shape, because the number of nuclei that could split hasn't changed. But a chain reaction depends on neutrons finding nuclei before they escape, and that depends on how far each fission is from the surface.

Some students think the sheet fails because its nuclei are spread further apart. They aren't: rolling the metal out doesn't change its density. It only makes the piece thinner, so far more of it lies close to a surface.

title: Hotter than the Sun

figure.alt: Empty HR diagram axes: luminosity, in units of the Sun's luminosity on a logarithmic scale, against surface temperature, which increases to the left. Only the Sun is marked, at a luminosity of 1 and a temperature of about 5800 K.

question: Star X has a higher surface temperature than the Sun. Treat both stars as black bodies. Which statement must be true?
options: X has a larger radius than the Sun
X is more luminous than the Sun
X has more mass than the Sun
X's spectrum peaks at a shorter wavelength than the Sun's
reveal:
Only the peak wavelength must be shorter. By Wien's displacement law, $\lambda_{\max} T = 2.9 \times 10^{-3}$ m K, so a higher surface temperature always means a shorter peak wavelength.

Luminosity depends on size as well as temperature: $L = \sigma A T^4$, where $A = 4\pi R^2$ is the surface area. A very small hot star can be far less luminous than the Sun.

On the HR diagram every star to the left of the Sun is hotter. That region includes the upper main sequence (stars bigger, more luminous and more massive than the Sun) but also the white dwarfs: hotter than the Sun, but only about the size of the Earth and much dimmer. Sirius B, for example, has a surface temperature of about 25 000 K, more than four times the Sun's, yet only a few hundredths of the Sun's luminosity. Most white dwarfs also have less mass than the Sun.

revealFigure.alt: The same HR diagram with the region to the left of the Sun shaded. The shaded region contains the upper part of the main sequence, above the Sun, and the white dwarfs, far below the Sun.
revealFigure.caption: Every star in the shaded region is hotter than the Sun. Stars there on the main sequence are more luminous than the Sun; white dwarfs are far less luminous. Positions are approximate.

tempting: Along the main sequence the pattern really is "hotter means bigger, more luminous and more massive", so it is tempting to apply it to every star. But that pattern belongs only to the main sequence. Temperature alone fixes a star's colour and peak wavelength; it doesn't fix its size or its luminosity, because the luminosity depends on the surface area too. White dwarfs break the pattern completely.

title: Who gets the energy?

figure.alt: Before: a deuterium nucleus (one proton, one neutron) and a tritium nucleus (one proton, two neutrons). An arrow leads to after: a helium-4 nucleus and a free neutron, each marked with a question mark.

question: In deuterium–tritium fusion, $^{2}_{1}\text{H} + {}^{3}_{1}\text{H} \rightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\text{He} + {}^{1}_{0}\text{n}$, about 17.6 MeV is released as kinetic energy of the two products. Before they fuse, the deuterium and tritium nuclei have very little momentum compared with the products. How is the 17.6 MeV shared?
options: Most goes to the neutron, because it has less mass
It is shared equally between the two products
Most goes to the helium-4 nucleus, because it has more mass
reveal:
The neutron gets about 80% of it, roughly 14.1 MeV, leaving about 3.5 MeV for the helium nucleus.

Momentum is conserved. The total momentum before is almost zero, so the two products fly apart with momenta of equal size in opposite directions. For the same momentum $p$, the kinetic energy is $E_k = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$, so the lighter particle gets more. The helium nucleus has about 4 times the neutron's mass, so the neutron moves about 4 times as fast and gets about 4 times as much kinetic energy: $\tfrac{4}{5} \times 17.6 \approx 14.1$ MeV, and $\tfrac{1}{5} \times 17.6 \approx 3.5$ MeV.

Beyond the syllabus: this matters in fusion reactors. Neutrons have no charge, so the magnetic field that holds the hot plasma can't hold them: they carry most of the energy out into the walls, where it is collected as thermal energy. The charged helium nuclei stay in the plasma and help to keep it hot.

revealFigure.alt: After the fusion, the helium-4 nucleus moves left with a short velocity arrow and 3.5 MeV; the neutron moves right with an arrow about four times as long and 14.1 MeV.
revealFigure.caption: Arrows show velocities. The products have equal and opposite momenta, so the neutron moves about 4 times as fast as the helium nucleus.

tempting: The helium nucleus is the "main" product and has most of the mass, so it seems it should take most of the energy. But the share is decided by conservation of momentum: the two products get momenta of equal size, and a light particle with a given momentum moves fast and carries more kinetic energy. An equal share would break momentum conservation, because equal kinetic energies with different masses would mean different momenta.

title: A fast cool star or a slow hot star?

figure.alt: A graph of intensity against wavelength in nanometres showing a single black-body curve that rises steeply, peaks at 500 nm and falls away slowly towards longer wavelengths. A question mark stands beside the peak.
figure.caption: The star's continuous spectrum, with its peak at 500 nm. The curve is calculated from Planck's law; the intensity scale is arbitrary.

question: An astronomer records the continuous spectrum of a star and finds that its intensity peaks at a wavelength of 500 nm. By Wien's displacement law that suggests a surface temperature of about 5800 K. A colleague objects: "A cooler star moving towards us fast enough would have its whole spectrum shifted to shorter wavelengths, and its peak could land at 500 nm too." Treating the star as a black body, can the shape of the continuous spectrum alone tell them which they are looking at: a 5800 K star at rest, or a cooler star approaching?
options: Yes: a Doppler-shifted black-body curve has a different shape, so the two cases can be told apart
No: a Doppler-shifted black-body curve is exactly a black-body curve for a different temperature, so only the spectral lines can settle it
Yes: a Doppler shift moves only the peak and leaves the rest of the curve where it was, which gives it away
No: nothing in a star's light can reveal how fast it is moving
reveal:
No. A shifted black-body curve is still a perfect black-body curve, so the continuous spectrum alone can only give an apparent temperature; the absorption lines settle it.

Wien's law, $\lambda_{\max} T = 2.9 \times 10^{-3}$ m K, gives 5800 K for a peak at 500 nm, and 580 nm for the peak of a 5000 K star. To bring that peak to 500 nm, every wavelength must be multiplied by $\dfrac{500}{580} = 0.86$, a fractional change $\dfrac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} = 0.14$, which with $\dfrac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} \approx \dfrac{v}{c}$ (C.5) means approaching at roughly $0.14c$ (the approximation is itself rough at such a speed, but the principle is what matters here).

The point is that a Doppler shift multiplies every wavelength by the same factor, and that is exactly what a change of temperature does to a black-body curve too: the shape of the curve depends on wavelength only through the product $\lambda T$ (plus an overall brightness factor). Shrink all the wavelengths of a 5000 K curve by 0.86 and you get precisely the curve of a 5800 K body, with its peak at 500 nm and the same shape on both sides. So from the continuous spectrum alone the two stars are indistinguishable.

What breaks the tie are the dark absorption lines, which are at wavelengths fixed by the atoms that make them. Hydrogen's red line, at 656 nm in the laboratory, would appear at 656 nm in the spectrum of the star at rest but at $656 \times 0.86 = 566$ nm for the approaching one. The line shift gives the speed (the C.5 understanding that shifts in spectral lines tell us about the motion of stars and galaxies), and once the speed is known every wavelength can be corrected and the true temperature read off.

In practice stars move at tens to hundreds of kilometres per second. At 100 $\text{km s}^{-1}$, $\dfrac{v}{c} = 3.3 \times 10^{-4}$, which changes an apparent 5800 K by only about 2 K, so for a star the correction hardly matters; the same lines are routinely used to measure the speeds of binary stars and the wobble caused by exoplanets. Beyond the course: for distant galaxies, and for the cosmic microwave background, the shifts are huge, and the shifted light is still a perfect black-body spectrum, which is part of how we know what it is.

revealFigure.alt: The same graph with two black-body curves lying exactly on top of each other: a solid curve for star A, 5800 kelvin at rest, and a dashed curve for star B, 5000 kelvin approaching fast. The same hydrogen absorption line is marked at 656 nm for star A and at 566 nm for star B.
revealFigure.caption: Star A: 5800 K, at rest. Star B: 5000 K, approaching at about 0.14c. The two continuous spectra are the same curve (B is dashed so that both show). Only the hydrogen absorption line, 656 nm in the laboratory, tells them apart: at 656 nm for A, shifted to 566 nm for B. Intensity scale arbitrary.

tempting:
"A shifted curve has a different shape" feels right because stretching or squeezing a graph usually distorts it. But a uniform scaling of all the wavelengths is exactly the change a black-body curve undergoes when its temperature changes, so the shifted curve lands precisely on another member of the same family.

"Only the peak moves" misreads the Doppler effect. Every wavelength changes by the same fraction $\dfrac{v}{c}$, not just the one at the peak, so the whole curve slides and squeezes together.

"Nothing in a star's light reveals its speed" forgets the spectral lines. Their laboratory wavelengths are known precisely, so their shift is one of astronomy's main tools for measuring how stars and galaxies move.

title: Precise or accurate?

figure.alt: Four number lines, labelled A to D, on a scale of g from 9.0 to 10.6 m s⁻². Each has five dots, one student's five measurements. A dashed line marks the true value, 9.8. Set A: five dots close together around 9.8. Set B: five dots close together around 9.3. Set C: dots spread widely, from about 9.4 to 10.2. Set D: dots spread widely, from about 9.9 to 10.6.
figure.caption: Each dot is one measurement of $g$. The dashed line is the true value, 9.8 $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

question: Four students each measure the acceleration of free fall, $g$, five times. The true value is 9.8 $\text{m s}^{-2}$. The picture shows each student's five results. Which set of results is precise but not accurate?
options: Set A
Set B
Set C
Set D
reveal:
Set B. Its five results are very close to each other (from 9.21 to 9.39 $\text{m s}^{-2}$), so it is precise. But they are all close to 9.3, not 9.8, so it isn't accurate: every result is about 0.5 $\text{m s}^{-2}$ too low. A shift like that, the same way for every reading, is the sign of a systematic error, such as a timer that always stops a little late, which makes every fall time too long.

Set A is precise and accurate. Set C is accurate on average (its mean is 9.80 $\text{m s}^{-2}$) but not precise: large random errors scatter its results. Set D is neither.

Skills: accuracy, precision and errors
tempting: The two words sound alike, and in everyday English they often mean the same thing. In physics they don't: precise means the results are close to each other; accurate means they are close to the true value. Set C is tempting because its results look untidy, and untidy feels "inaccurate", but they are spread evenly around 9.8. Set B looks the most professional of all, and that's the trap: a tight group of results is no guarantee that they are right.

title: The worn ruler

figure.alt: A ruler numbered in centimetres whose left end is worn away, so the zero mark is missing. An eraser lies on the ruler with one end lined up with the worn end of the ruler.
figure.caption: The worn end of the ruler is where the 2 mm mark would be.

question: The end of a student's ruler is worn away, so its zero mark has gone: the end is now where the 2 mm mark would be. She measures the length of an eraser by lining up one end of it with the end of the ruler and reading the scale at the other end. She takes 10 readings and uses their mean. Which statement is correct?
options: Each reading is 2 mm too short, and taking the mean of 10 removes the error
Each reading is 2 mm too long, and taking the mean of 10 removes the error
Each reading is 2 mm too short, and taking the mean of 10 doesn't change the error
Each reading is 2 mm too long, and taking the mean of 10 doesn't change the error
reveal:
Each reading is 2 mm too long, and repeating doesn't change that. The eraser starts at the worn end, where the scale would read 2 mm, so the reading at its other end is its true length plus 2 mm. The error is systematic: every reading is 2 mm too long, so the mean of 10 readings is also 2 mm too long. Taking a mean reduces only random errors, which push some readings up and others down, so that they partly cancel. A systematic error pushes every reading the same way, so nothing cancels.

To fix it, deal with the cause. Subtract 2 mm from every reading, or measure from a clear mark, such as the 1 cm mark, and subtract the two readings (as for any length measured on a ruler, the uncertainty is ±1 mm).

Skills: accuracy, precision and errors
tempting: "Too short" is tempting because something is missing from the ruler, so it feels as if the readings must come out small. But the missing part is at the start of the scale: the eraser begins at the 2 mm position, so the scale counts 2 mm that aren't there. "Repeat and take the mean" is the standard advice for improving a result, so it's tempting to think it fixes any error, or at least shrinks it. It works only for random errors. Here the 10 readings will agree closely with each other (they are precise), which can make the result look trustworthy when every one of them is wrong by the same 2 mm.

title: Through the origin?

figure.alt: A graph of current I in amperes, from 0 to 0.18, against potential difference V in volts, from 0 to 7. Six data points, at 1 V to 6 V, each with a vertical uncertainty bar. The points rise steadily, from about 0.06 A at 1 V to about 0.16 A at 6 V. No line is drawn.
figure.caption: Each uncertainty bar is ±0.01 A. The uncertainty in $V$ is too small to show.

question: A student measures the current $I$ in a resistor for six values of the potential difference $V$ across it. Theory says that $I$ is proportional to $V$, because the resistance stays constant. She plots her data with an uncertainty bar on every point, as in the picture. The points lie close to a straight line, but that line would cross the current axis above zero. How should she draw her line of best fit?
options: Draw the best straight line through the points (within the uncertainty bars), even if it misses the origin
Draw the line through the origin anyway, because the theory says so
Leave out the points that don't fit a line through the origin
Join the points dot-to-dot
reveal:
Draw the best straight line through the uncertainty bars, and let it miss the origin. The line must follow the data, not the theory. Here it passes through every uncertainty bar and crosses the current axis at about 0.04 A.

An intercept that should be zero but isn't is evidence of a systematic error. Here it is probably a zero error: an ammeter whose pointer sits at 0.04 A when no current flows adds 0.04 A to every reading. That shifts the whole line up without changing its slope, so the gradient is still valid. The gradient is about 0.020 $\text{A V}^{-1}$, so the resistance is $R = \dfrac{1}{0.020} = 50$ Ω. Report the intercept and suggest a cause: it's useful information, not a failure.

Skills: graphs and best-fit lines · Skills: what an intercept means

revealFigure.alt: The same graph with a solid best-fit line that passes through every uncertainty bar and crosses the current axis at about 0.04 A, which is circled. A dashed orange line forced through the origin misses four of the six uncertainty bars.
revealFigure.caption: The best-fit line (black) crosses the current axis at about 0.04 A (circled). A line forced through the origin misses four of the six uncertainty bars.

tempting: It's tempting to trust the theory over the data, or to treat the points that "spoil" a line through the origin as mistakes. But the theory describes an ideal experiment, and your line must describe your data. Leaving points out so that the data fit a theory is never acceptable. Joining the dots is tempting because it passes through every point exactly, but it treats random scatter as if it were real, and it doesn't give a single gradient.

title: Adding 3 N and 4 N

figure.alt: Two arrows start from a small ring: a 4.0 N force pointing right and a 3.0 N force pointing up and to the right. The angle between them is marked with a question mark.
figure.caption: Seen from above. You choose the angle between the two forces.

question: Two forces, of 3.0 N and 4.0 N, act on the same small ring. You can choose the angle between them. Which of these can not be the size of the resultant of these two forces?
reveal:
8.0 N. Forces are vectors: they add tip to tail, so their directions matter. The resultant is largest when the two forces point the same way, $4.0 + 3.0 = 7.0$ N, and smallest when they point in opposite directions, $4.0 - 3.0 = 1.0$ N. Every angle in between gives a resultant somewhere between 1.0 N and 7.0 N. At right angles it is $\sqrt{3.0^2 + 4.0^2} = 5.0$ N.

No angle can make the resultant bigger than 7.0 N: one side of a triangle is never longer than the other two sides together.

Skills: vectors

revealFigure.alt: The 4.0 N force drawn as an arrow, with a dashed circle of radius 3.0 N around its tip. The 3.0 N force, added tip to tail, can end anywhere on the circle, here at right angles. The resultant runs from the start to that point: 5.0 N. Dots on the circle mark 7.0 N on the far side and 1.0 N on the near side.
revealFigure.caption: Drawn to scale. Adding the 3.0 N force to the 4.0 N force tip to tail: as you turn it, the tip of the resultant moves round the dashed circle, so the resultant can be anything from 1.0 N to 7.0 N (5.0 N at right angles).

tempting: Two ideas are common: that forces simply add, so the resultant "must" be 7.0 N, or that the answer "must" be 5.0 N, because the 3–4–5 triangle is so familiar. Either way, the other values look impossible. But the resultant depends on the angle between the forces: 7.0 N needs them in the same direction, 5.0 N at right angles, and 1.0 N in opposite directions. Only 8.0 N is out of reach.

title: Timing 20 swings

figure.alt: A pendulum hanging from a stand, with a dashed outline showing the other end of its swing, labelled 20 swings. Beside it, a stopwatch reads 31.40.
figure.caption: One swing is a complete oscillation, there and back.

question: A student times 20 complete swings of a pendulum. Her stopwatch reads 31.40 s, but her reaction time makes the total time uncertain by about ±0.2 s, so she records $t = (31.4 \pm 0.2)$ s. What is the uncertainty in the period, the time for one swing?
reveal:
±0.01 s. One period is $T = \dfrac{31.4}{20} = 1.570$ s. The 20 is an exact count, with no uncertainty, so dividing by it divides the absolute uncertainty by 20 as well: $\Delta T = \dfrac{0.2}{20} = 0.01$ s. So $T = (1.57 \pm 0.01)$ s.

The percentage uncertainty doesn't change: $\dfrac{0.2}{31.4} = 0.6\%$ and $\dfrac{0.01}{1.57} = 0.6\%$. This is why we time many swings: the reaction-time error happens only when you start and stop the stopwatch, however many swings you count, so it is shared among all of them.

Skills: propagating uncertainties
tempting: ±0.2 s is tempting because that was the uncertainty in the timing, and it feels as if it must carry over unchanged. But the ±0.2 s belongs to the whole 31.4 s, not to each swing. ±0.1 s comes from sharing the uncertainty between starting and stopping, rather than among the 20 swings. ±4 s comes from multiplying by 20 instead of dividing, which would make one swing more uncertain than all 20 together.

title: Dividing by T squared

figure.alt: A pendulum hanging from a clamp. Its length l is marked as measured precisely, and its period is given as T = (1.57 ± 0.01) s.
figure.caption: The period from "Timing 20 swings", used to find $g$.

question: A student finds the period of a pendulum to be $T = (1.57 \pm 0.01)$ s, a percentage uncertainty of about 0.6%. Its length $l$ is measured so precisely that its uncertainty can be ignored. She calculates $g$ from $g = \dfrac{4\pi^2 l}{T^2}$. What is the percentage uncertainty in $g$?
reveal:
About 1.3%. $g$ depends on $T^{-2}$. For a power, multiply the fractional uncertainty by the size of the power; the minus sign doesn't make it any smaller. So $\dfrac{\Delta g}{g} = 2 \times \dfrac{\Delta T}{T} = 2 \times \dfrac{0.01}{1.57} = 2 \times 0.64\% \approx 1.3\%$. The 4 and $\pi^2$ are exact numbers, and the uncertainty in $l$ is negligible, so they add nothing.

Dividing by $T^2$ is dividing by $T$ twice, and dividing (like multiplying) adds percentage uncertainties: $0.64\% + 0.64\%$. With numbers, if $l = 0.612$ m, then $g = \dfrac{4\pi^2 \times 0.612}{1.57^2} = 9.80$ $\text{m s}^{-2}$, and 1.3% of that is 0.12, so $g = (9.8 \pm 0.1)$ $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

Skills: propagating uncertainties
tempting: 0.6% is tempting because only one quantity, $T$, carries an uncertainty, so it seems to carry straight over. But $T$ appears twice in $T^2$, so its uncertainty counts twice. 0.3% comes from thinking that dividing makes an uncertainty smaller (halving is the rule for a square root, not for dividing by a square). 2.5% comes from multiplying by 4, as if the 4 in the equation or the square of the power mattered.

title: Both ends of the ruler

figure.alt: A pencil lying just above a ruler marked in millimetres and numbered in centimetres. The end of the pencil lines up with 12.0 mm and its tip with 155.0 mm.
figure.caption: The ruler is numbered in centimetres and marked every millimetre.

question: A student measures a pencil with a millimetre ruler, without starting at zero: the end of the pencil is at 12.0 mm and its tip is at 155.0 mm. What is the uncertainty in the pencil's length?
options: ±1 mm
±2 mm
±5 mm
reveal:
±1 mm. The length is the difference between two readings: $155.0 - 12.0 = 143.0$ mm. Each reading on an analogue scale is uncertain by half the smallest division, ±0.5 mm. When you subtract two values, their absolute uncertainties add: $0.5 + 0.5 = 1$ mm. So the length is $(143 \pm 1)$ mm.

The same is true when you line one end up with the zero mark: judging where the zero is still counts as a reading. That's why a length measured with a ruler is always ± one full division.

Skills: recording uncertainties
tempting: ±0.5 mm is tempting because "half the smallest division" is the rule for a single reading on an analogue scale. But a length needs two readings, one at each end, and each has its own ±0.5 mm. ±2 mm and ±5 mm (half a centimetre) are too pessimistic: you can judge each end to within half a millimetre.

title: The drone in the wind

figure.alt: Top view of a drone pointing due north, towards a flag directly ahead of it. A blue arrow shows the drone's velocity relative to the air, 3.0 m s⁻¹ north. An orange arrow shows the wind, 4.0 m s⁻¹ towards the east.
figure.caption: Seen from above. The blue arrow is the drone's velocity relative to the air; the orange arrow is the wind. Not to scale.

question: A small drone flies pointing due north, at 3.0 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ relative to the air. A steady wind blows the air towards the east at 4.0 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. What is the drone's speed relative to the ground? Will it reach the flag directly north of where it started?
reveal:
5.0 $\text{m s}^{-1}$, and it misses the flag. The drone's velocity relative to the ground is its velocity relative to the air plus the air's velocity relative to the ground. These are at right angles, so $v = \sqrt{3.0^2 + 4.0^2} = 5.0$ $\text{m s}^{-1}$, in a direction $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{4.0}{3.0}\right) = 53°$ east of north. Pointing north doesn't make it travel north: it drifts east. If the flag is 30 m away, the drone takes 10 s to cover 30 m northwards, and in that time the wind carries it 40 m east.

Could it reach the flag by pointing partly into the wind? Not in this wind. To cancel the 4.0 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ drift it would need a westward component of 4.0 $\text{m s}^{-1}$, more than its whole speed relative to the air. Whichever way it points, it is carried east of the flag.

A.1: relative velocity · Skills: vectors

revealFigure.alt: Vector triangle: a 3.0 m s⁻¹ arrow pointing north, then a 4.0 m s⁻¹ arrow pointing east from its tip. The resultant, 5.0 m s⁻¹, runs from the start to the end, at 53 degrees east of north.
revealFigure.caption: Drawn to scale, tip to tail: the velocity relative to the air plus the velocity of the air gives the velocity relative to the ground (black).

tempting: It's tempting to think that pointing at the flag means flying to it, or that the two speeds simply add to 7.0 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ (or subtract to 1.0 $\text{m s}^{-1}$). But the wind carries the whole drone sideways whichever way it points, and velocities at right angles add as vectors, by Pythagoras. Another common idea is that a cross-wind slows the drone down. Here it actually makes the drone faster relative to the ground, just in the wrong direction.

title: What the gradient means

figure.alt: Axes with v squared, in m² s⁻², up the side and s, in m, along the bottom, and a straight line rising from the origin. There are no numbers on the axes.

question: A trolley starts from rest and rolls down a ramp with a constant acceleration $a$. A light gate measures its speed $v$ after it has travelled a distance $s$ down the ramp, for several different distances. A graph of $v^2$ against $s$ is a straight line through the origin. What does its gradient equal?
options: $\tfrac{1}{2}a$
$\sqrt{2a}$
reveal:
$2a$. For uniform acceleration from rest, $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with $u = 0$, so $v^2 = 2as$. Compare this with $y = mx$: $y$ is $v^2$, $x$ is $s$, and the gradient $m$ is $2a$. The units agree: $\text{m}^2\,\text{s}^{-2}$ divided by m gives $\text{m s}^{-2}$, the unit of an acceleration. So the trolley's acceleration is half the gradient: a gradient of 1.6 $\text{m s}^{-2}$ means $a = 0.80$ $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

To find what any gradient means, write the equation with the $y$-axis quantity on its own on one side, then see what multiplies the $x$-axis quantity.

Skills: linearising and logarithms
tempting: $a$ is tempting because the trolley's acceleration is $a$, and it feels as if the gradient of any graph about motion should be the acceleration. But the gradient is whatever multiplies the $x$-axis quantity in the equation, and that depends on what you plot. $\tfrac{1}{2}a$ is the gradient of a different graph, $s$ against $t^2$ (from $s = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$), which is easy to mix up with this one. $\sqrt{2a}$ would be the gradient of $v$ against $\sqrt{s}$.
